news.title: The week in whoppers: Mamdani inverts reality to push a government takeover, Newsom puts words in Trump’s mouth and more
news.text:
Diary of disturbing disinformation and dangerous delusions

This definition

“Socialism . . . means that you will have whatever you need to live a dignified life and that it is the government’s job to deliver on that.” — Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Friday

We say: This is Mamdani’s pitch to let government take charge of everything. 

Hmm: Has he ever been to a Motor Vehicles office? Does he think living on the dole is dignified

Government has never delivered “dignity,” which comes from pride in doing, not getting.

This warning

“Let’s be clear: The President is advocating for an attack on 10+ million US residents in two of America’s largest cities.” — Calif. Gov. Gavin Newsom, Monday

We say: Let’s be clear: President Trump advocated for no such thing.

The left is portraying his remark that higher gas prices are a small price to pay for ending the Iranian nuclear threat as a sign that he’s deranged — by taking his words out of context and then twisting them.

That kind of desperate attack suggests they’re struggling to find any legitimate criticism. 

This advice

“When you feel powerless, you are powerless. And when you feel powerful, you are powerful. And we are powerful.” — Former Vice President Kamala Harris, Sunday

We say: Kamala thinks wishing hard enough and clicking her heels together will get her to the White House. 

Too bad the Power of Positive Feeling doesn’t extend to winning elections. Maybe she should leave politics and become a motivational speaker instead.

“Our laws do not allow for criminals to have sanctuary.” — Gov. Kathy Hochul, Tuesday

We say: New York state law, in fact, provides sanctuary to thousands of illegal alien criminals — including murderers and sexual predators — by releasing them from custody despite federal requests for their removal. 

How dumb does Hochul think New Yorkers are?

— Compiled by The Post Editorial Board
news.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani provided his own curious definition of socialism — that involves the government having to do everything.

news.title: Abdul El-Sayed responds to President Trump's Truth Social attack
news.text:
Michigan Senate Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed snapped back at President Donald Trump's late-night Islamophobic Truth Social tirade, where he repeatedly called him "Mohammed" and a "terrorist sympathizer."

The night before the first Senate debate between El-Sayed and Republican Senate candidate Rep. Mike Rogers, Trump on Oct. 7 also called El-Sayed "a RADICAL Extremist," adding that "Mohammed’s Values are not exactly those of Michiganders, or those of our Great United States of America!" The president reiterated his "TOTAL ENDORSEMENT" for Rogers.

El-Sayed, seeking to be the first Muslim U.S. senator, responded Oct. 8, saying Trump knows his "name is Abdul" and that the president says it daily.

"But he’s not just attacking me. He’s attacking all of us. He thinks so low of us," El-Sayed said about the president in a post on X. "He thinks he can use my name and my faith to distract us from the suffering his policies are inflicting on us at the pump, at the grocery store, and at the doctor’s office. He thinks we don’t know any better.

"It’s time for change," added El-Sayed, a former public health official who won a contentious Democratic Senate primary against Rep. Hayley Stevens in August to secure the Democratic nomination for Senate.

Trump's comments and El-Sayed's response come as many polls show a tight race between El-Sayed and Rogers, capturing national attention as the Senate election is critical to Democrats' quest to take control of the Senate. Their Oct. 8 debate arrives as more than 200,000 Michiganders have already cast absentee ballots.

Who is Abdul El-Sayed?: The physician's path to the Dems' Michigan Senate nomination

El-Sayed, Rogers finally scheduled for first debate

A day after winning the Democratic Senate primary, El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants whose full name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, sent a message to Rogers, Trump and other Republicans during his victory speech ahead of possible attacks during the campaign trail.

"They think they want to use my whole name against me. Mike, listen, man, if you can’t say the name — it’s Abdulrahman — keep the name out of your damn mouth," El-Sayed said. "I’ll be happy to give you lessons." 

Also at that speech, El-Sayed challenged Rogers to five debates. Although Rogers skipped a Sept. 15 debate against El-Sayed in Detroit over moderator issues, the two candidates are scheduled to finally take the stage Oct. 8 in Grand Rapids for their first face-to-face encounter.

A progressive and self-proclaimed capitalist candidate endorsed by former President Barack Obama, former Vice President Kamala Harris, and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vermont, El-Sayed has energized fellow progressives and young voters. However, El-Sayed has some moderate Democrats concerned about his views, his tense relations with local Jewish communities and his ability to win retiring Democrat Sen. Gary Peters' seat against Rogers.
news.author: Usa Today

news.title: Republicans Blame Trump for High Costs in Two Key Senate Battlegrounds
news.text: Many Republicans in Iowa and Ohio are blaming President Donald Trump’s policies for rising costs ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, according to a new CNN/SSRS poll released Thursday. Fifty percent of Iowa Republicans and 49 percent of Ohio Republicans said Trump’s policies “increased the cost of living” in the new poll, which comes as the two states emerge as critical midterm battlegrounds despite the states backing Trump in all three of his presidential runs. Both states have competitive Senate and governor’s races in this year’s midterms. Control of the House and Senate could come down to these two Midwestern states. Both are former battlegrounds, having given their electoral votes to former President Barack Obama in 2008 and 2012 before shifting rightward during the Trump era. Trump’s inroads with white, rural voters helped move these states to the Republican column. But Democrats believe dissatisfaction with the economy during Trump’s second term in office could give them the opportunity to win back voters to make the states competitive again this year. Historically, the party in the White House loses seats when the president’s approval rating is low, and recent polls have found Trump’s numbers falling to their lowest point of his second term, fueling Democrats’ optimism about their chances of competing in states like Iowa and Ohio. The economy has become a “significant drag on Republican prospects” because there is a “very close link” to how people feel about their personal finances and how they vote in elections, Costas Panagopoulos, professor of political science at Northeastern University, told Newsweek. “If even the president's own supporters are blaming him for these issues, there's the likelihood that they will either defect to Democratic candidates in the midterms or not vote at all, which could be equally problematic,” he said. “Voters are connecting the dots.” Cultural issues, which have been used as “wedge issues” in campaigns, have become “secondary” to the “economic pain” voters are dealing with in this election, he said. In Iowa, Republican Representative Ashley Hinson and Democratic state Representative Josh Turek are competing in a Senate race, while Democratic state Auditor Rob Sand and Republican Zach Lahn are running in the gubernatorial race. Ohio races are also highly competitive. In the Senate race, Republican Senator Jon Husted is facing a challenge from former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown. Meanwhile, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy and Democrat Amy Acton are running in the gubernatorial race. White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told Newsweek that nobody “can dispute the fact that President Trump has created one of the most robust coalitions in political history with the MAGA movement.” “President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress,” he said. Iowa and Ohio Voters Blame Trump Policies for Rising Prices Across all voter groups, 74 percent of voters in Iowa and 76 percent of voters in Ohio believe Trump’s policies have increased the cost of living, according to the new polls from CNN. Fifty-five percent in Iowa and 58 percent in Ohio said they believe that Trump’s tariffs are a “bad thing” for their state, while 70 percent in Iowa and 68 percent in Ohio said the recent increase in gas prices, which have soared amid the Iran war, has caused personal hardship for them. Both polls were conducted from September 29 to October 5. The Iowa poll surveyed 801 respondents and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.2 percentage points, while the Ohio poll surveyed 760 respondents and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.5 percentage points. Trump won both states by double digits in the 2024 election. He won Ohio by about 11 points and Iowa by about 13 points over former Vice President Kamala Harris. What Polls Show About Iowa, Ohio Races The polls pointed to competitive races in both states. Hinson held a 2-point lead in the Iowa Senate race over Turek, 45 percent to 43 percent. However, in the gubernatorial race, Sand held a 9-point lead over Lahn, 51 percent to 42 percent. Democrats had an advantage in both statewide races in Ohio. Brown led Husted by 6 points, 49 percent to 43 percent, in the Senate race, while Acton held an 8-point lead, 50 percent to 42 percent, over Ramaswamy in the gubernatorial race, according to the poll. The economic fallout of Trump’s policies gives Democrats a chance to persuade some Republicans to vote for their candidates, but Democrats should not necessarily expect to win “large segments of the Republican population,” Panagopoulos said. Its impact on turnout will be critically important, he said. “What we're seeing is lots of enthusiasm in this election cycle around Democrats, around the prospects of winning in November and putting the brakes on some of these Republican policies,” he said. “That enthusiasm often translates into higher turnout amongst those voters in elections. We're seeing comparatively lower levels of enthusiasm among Republicans.” Why Iowa and Ohio Appear Competitive Again These two former battlegrounds appear competitive in this election cycle as Democrats hope to expand the electoral playing field into more conservative states. The economy is a central reason Democrats believe these states may be competitive. Voter beliefs that Trump’s policies have driven up the cost of living and that tariffs are hurting their states could weaken Republicans in the states. Republicans have long held an advantage over Democrats in terms of voter perceptions of the economy, and Americans often vote based on economic conditions, so a shift in that perception could leave the GOP more vulnerable in places they’ve performed well in recent elections. Trump has done well with white voters in rural areas in both states. This voting bloc was previously more competitive, but the Democratic collapse among them has been a main factor driving them into Republican control. Democrats have gained ground in suburban areas in those states, but have not made strong enough inroads to offset their rural losses. Democrats have struggled statewide in both of these states. Sand and Brown are among the only Democrats who have managed to win statewide races in either state during the Trump era. Sand and Brown running again in 2026, a more favorable national environment, has bolstered Democrats’ hopes of flipping those states. Iowa is a major agricultural exporter of goods like corn and soybeans, and farmers may feel the squeeze from tariffs and diesel prices. Meanwhile, data centers have become a sticking point in Ohio especially, tying into broader themes of affordability that have defined the midterms. The Senate races in these two states are especially important. Democrats are hoping to flip control of the chamber, where Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority, but have limited pickup opportunities in traditionally competitive states. This means they need to compete in double-digit Trump states to win a majority. As these two states do have a history of backing Democrats as recently as the 2010s, they have become some of the most hotly contested races that could ultimately decide whether Democrats or Republicans win control of the Senate after the midterms. Donald Trump Approval Rating Trump’s approval rating was also underwater in both states. In Iowa, his approval stood at -17 points, 41 percent approving and 58 percent disapproving of his job performance. Over in Ohio, his net approval rating was -28 points, with 36 percent approving and 64 percent disapproving. Two recent national polls shed light on Trump’s standing nationwide. Only 36 percent of Americans approved of Trump, while 64 percent disapproved of him, in a new Reuters/Ipsos poll of 3,526 registered voters. Meanwhile, his approval stood at 38 percent, with 60 percent disapproving of him, in a new YouGov/The Economist poll of 1,381 registered voters. His approval among Republicans was still strong in both of those polls. Seventy-seven percent of Republicans in the Reuters/Ipsos poll and 79 percent of Republicans in the YouGov poll approved of Trump. The Reuters/Ipsos poll was conducted from September 30 to October 5 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 1.7 percentage points among registered voters. The YouGov poll was conducted from October 2 to 5 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.4 percentage points. What Happens Next Trump’s standing among Republicans will have major implications for the midterms. The president will want to retain positive numbers with his core base of supporters to ensure they head to the polls. Issues like the economy, cost of living and gas prices could impact how Americans view his presidency. Panagopoulos said it is likely too late for Republicans to change the narrative about the economy. “Millions of votes have already been cast. These views are baked in the minds of the electorate at this point and what they can do is focus on mobilizing supporters to get to the polls,” he said.
news.summary: Republicans are blaming Trump policies for increasing the cost of living in Iowa and Ohio, a new poll found ahead of the midterms.
news.author: Andrew Stanton

news.title: Trump voters not excited for midterms as approval rating slips: Poll
news.text:
With critical midterm elections only weeks away, fewer than one-third of 2024 Trump voters say they are enthusiastic about voting in November, a potential sign that the president's base is eroding, according to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll.

The poll, completed on Monday, Oct. 5, found that only 30% of 2024 Trump voters were “very enthusiastic” to vote in November, compared with 48% of people who voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted over a six-day period among 4,506 adults online, has a margin of error of plus or minus 2 percentage points.

Monday’s poll is the most recent sign of a crumbling coalition for Trump, who also saw a decline in Hispanic American support in another Reuters/Ipsos poll released the same day.

A continued drop

Since the start of his second term in the White House in 2025, Trump's support among every major demographic group has dropped, including double-digit drops among Hispanics, men, rural and suburban voters, people without college degrees and evangelical Christians.

Among male voters, a group Trump carried in all three of his presidential campaigns, the drop is more notable, with the demographic backing the Democrats over the Republicans 43% to 39%, according to Reuters/Ipsos.

That four-point gap is the largest Reuters/Ipsos has recorded during Trump’s second administration.

More: How Americans rank Trump among US presidents

Cost of living amid opposition to Trump

Monday’s poll also found that cost of living ranks as the top issue on voters' minds heading into November. Democratic values ranked second, followed by immigration as the top three issues voters were concerned with.

Reuters/Ipsos also found that a large majority of enthusiastic voters looked forward to opposing the president, with 62% expressing that sentiment. Meanwhile, only 36% said they were eager to support the president in November.

What do polling averages show?

While individual polls vary, major polling averages continue to show Trump deeply underwater, with disapproval ratings approaching or exceeding 60% nationally.

RealClearPolitics (Oct. 8): 38.3% approve, 59.5% disapproveNew York Times (Oct. 8): 37% approve, 60% disapproveSilver Bulletin (Oct. 8): 37.1% approve, 60.1% disapprove

Reuters contributed to the reporting of this story.

Fernando Cervantes Jr. is a trending news reporter for USA TODAY. Reach him at fernando.cervantes@usatodayco.com and follow him on X @fern_cerv_.

news.title: Trump announces tornado aid for Menasha after CBS News report
news.text: Wisconsin is set to receive nearly $18 million in federal disaster aid after weeks of waiting following a devastating tornado in Menasha.President Trump said on Truth Social that he approved the aid after speaking with Wisconsin Rep. Tom Tiffany, the state's Republican candidate for governor.The announcement came one day after "CBS Mornings" aired CBS News chief medical correspondent Dr. Jon LaPook's report on residents still awaiting federal assistance, which Democratic Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers formally requested on Aug. 26. LaPook's report cited an analysis of FEMA data that found Mr. Trump approved 85% of disaster aid requests from states he won in 2024, compared with only 46% of requests from states won by Kamala Harris. States with Democratic governors also appeared to fare worse. Wisconsin, which Trump won in 2024, has a Democratic governor.The White House denied Wednesday that politics played a role, telling CBS News in a statement, "There is no politicization to the President's decisions on disaster relief and the president responds to each request with great care and consideration."The powerful EF-3 tornado damaged or destroyed more than 1,000 buildings in Menasha in July, carving a 14-mile path of destruction over more than 20 minutes, according to the National Weather Service. Miraculously, no one died.Last weekend, thousands of people came together as filmmaker Phil Johnston and a team of volunteers organized a benefit concert for Menasha, with "Menasha Strong" becoming the rallying cry. Wisconsin's disaster fund does not provide money directly to residents to cover their losses, leaving local governments — which have limited resources of their own — to provide that assistance."People are upset that the government isn't helping a whole lot," Johnston told LaPook at the fundraiser Saturday. "It shouldn't have to be a fundraising concert that is giving you basic needs to live your life. It's not right."Menasha residents described feeling "levitated" and "gobsmacked" by the news, LaPook said Thursday.Comedian Charlie Berens, who emceed the event, said the federal funding was a long time coming."If I was a beer half empty guy, I'd say Menasha deserved this money months ago. But being the beer half full guy I am, I just want to say, when neighbors stick together and help their neighbors, good things can happen," he said.
news.summary: President Trump announced nearly $18 million in federal disaster aid for Wisconsin one day after CBS News reported on residents still waiting for aid following a devastating tornado.
news.author: Dr. Jon Lapook

news.title: Abdul El-Sayed Criticized Obama. Is That a Scandal?
news.text:
When Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign announced that Barack Obama would join him on the campaign trail later this month, media outlets and prominent online voices quickly sounded the alarm—the Michigan Senate candidate, it turned out, had voiced strong criticisms of the former president. 

On Wednesday, CNN traced El-Sayed’s comments from the time of Obama’s 2012 reelection through the 2020 presidential campaign, zeroing in on a 2012 HuffPost piece where El-Sayed wrote that the former president did not deliver on the promise of “hope and substantial change” during his first term but instead “perpetuated war, violated our civil liberties, deported more people from our shores than any other president before him.” “The list of his failures,” El-Sayed wrote, “goes on.” 

It’s not that people are calling El-Sayed’s criticisms wrong. They’re pointing out that they exist.

In a statement to CNN, El-Sayed praised Obama: “He changed what was possible for someone like me, with a name like mine.” 

“Despite all he did, there remains so much left to do,” he added. “That’s where the next generation, inspired by him and his leadership, picks up.”

The New York Post extended the supposed concerns to other Democrats, pointing again to El-Sayed campaigning with former Vice President Kamala Harris on Thursday, despite El-Sayed publicly endorsing the Uncommitted movement in 2024, supporting calls for Democrats to withhold their primary votes from Joe Biden in protest of US military aid to Israel in its ongoing genocide in Gaza. While the movement declined to endorse Harris ahead of the national election—instead urging supporters to “vote against” Trump—El-Sayed actually did endorse her, in a marked break.

El-Sayed, the implication runs, is not such a good friend to his fellow Democrats after all. But intense critiques of Obama are something he has in common with both wings of his party. Countless Democrats and progressives have previously criticized Obama, in private and in public, from the former president’s left and right flanks, and supported him afterward (or, for some of those who actually held national office at the time, during). In party politics, done right, political alliances cut across ideological and policy disagreements. That’s just strategic campaigning—which Obama still plans to do alongside El-Sayed in October.

news.title: Trump’s Worst Nightmare Comes True as His Own Voters Check Out
news.text:
Donald Trump is practically begging his supporters to pretend he is on the ballot this November, but a new poll suggests the pitch is falling flat.

The president, 80, has repeatedly urged Republicans to treat the midterms as a referendum on his second term, apparently betting that putting himself at the center of the elections will energize the MAGA base and drive Republicans to the polls.

At a rally in Nebraska on Monday, he made that message explicit.

“When I am on the ballot, people show up and we always win,” Trump said. “I am asking you to do me a favor and pretend I am on the ballot.”

Later, he put it more simply: “In a true way, I am running. We have to keep it going.”

But a new Reuters/Ipsos poll points to a potentially serious problem for that strategy: Trump voters are far less enthusiastic about voting than the voters he defeated in 2024.

Just 30 percent of people who voted for Trump in 2024 said they were “very enthusiastic” about casting a ballot in this year’s midterms. Among voters who backed Kamala Harris, the figure was 48 percent.

That 18-point enthusiasm gap could be particularly consequential in a midterm election, when turnout is typically lower than in presidential contests.

And among voters who are enthusiastic about November’s election, opposition to Trump appears to be a more powerful motivator than support for him. Sixty-two percent said they were excited to vote against Trump, compared with 36 percent who said they were eager to support him.

Republican strategist Charlie Gerow acknowledged the challenge, telling Reuters: “The enthusiasm has to be ginned up among Republicans because turnout is what’s going to determine the outcome of these midterm elections.”

The poll also found that Trump’s supporters are less settled on their congressional choices. While most Trump and Harris voters intend to support candidates from their respective parties, 13 percent of Trump voters said they were still unsure who they would vote for, compared with 7 percent of Harris voters.

That is not the only poll that has shown such a result.

A New York Times/Siena poll last month found Democrats held an edge in voter certainty, with 61 percent saying they were absolutely certain to vote compared with 56 percent of Republicans.

For some Trump voters, the problem is not simply a lack of enthusiasm—it is outright disengagement.

Jim Pasek, an 80-year-old Michigan voter who has supported Trump twice, said the president’s recent statements leave him confused and frustrated.

“He’s not making sense,” Pasek told The New York Times. “It confuses me, and then I just get disgusted and tune out.”

In Texas, 24-year-old Brandon Tremaine, who voted for Trump in 2020, went even further after Trump urged supporters to vote as though he were on the ballot.

“President Trump has been saying, ‘Vote as if I was on the ballot,’ and that’s exactly what I’m going to do—not vote,” Tremaine said.

Republican organizer Doug Koopman said the problem is visible on the ground, too, describing low energy among volunteers in Michigan and saying campaign literature was sitting untouched at party headquarters.

“There’s very low energy on the Republican side,” he said.

It comes as polls suggest the Republicans are set to face a difficult midterms.

Pollster Angus Reid has Democrats up 16 points on the generic congressional ballot—their biggest lead yet, although other polling organizations put the lead at around 9 points.

Many believe that is because voters are not impressed with Trump’s leadership.

Political analyst Charlie Cook has argued that the election is not about a rising Democratic tide, but a weakening Trump brand.

He described the dynamic as a “red undertow” that could “pull many Republicans under.”

The tide has been turning against Trump and his party ever since he launched his deeply unpopular war on Iran in February.

The war has caused energy prices to spike. AAA figures show the average price of fuel in the U.S. at $4.37 a gallon, while diesel stands at $6.32.

Food prices have also risen, with ground beef up 7.2 percent over the past 12 months, while seafood, sugar, and coffee are all up around 6 percent, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

And Americans—including Trump voters—are not happy about it.

“He says it’s chump change. No, it’s not! It’s killing the people,” Pasek said about gas prices. “He’s losing touch with the American people,”

Tremaine told the New York Times: “You do not campaign on being the ticket of peace and start a war of choice that is directly hurting Americans here at home and gotten Americans killed overseas.”

Al Pscholka, a Republican and former member of the Michigan House of Representatives, added: “People are tired. The whole ‘divider-in-chief’ thing has gotten to the point where it’s just exhausting.”

The Reuters/Ipsos survey showed that Trump’s approval rating sits at just 32 percent.

And among men—a group Trump carried in all three of his presidential campaigns—Democrats now lead Republicans 43 percent to 39 percent when voters are asked how they would vote in a congressional race.

The Daily Beast has contacted the White House for comment.
news.summary:
Kevin Dietsch / Getty ImagesDonald Trump is practically begging his supporters to pretend he is on the ballot this November, but a new poll suggests the pitch is falling flat.

The president, 80, has repeatedly urged Republicans to treat the midterms as a referendum on his second term, apparently betting that putting himself at the center of the elections will energize the MAGA base and drive Republicans to the polls.

At a rally in Nebraska on Monday, he made that message explicit.

Read more at The Daily Beast.
news.author: Martha McHardy

news.title: Risk Facing Sherrod Brown’s Youth Vote Strategy
news.text: Sherrod Brown is courting young Ohioans in the Buckeye State’s U.S. Senate race as polls give the Democrat commanding age-group leads but identify weak voting enthusiasm as a potential vulnerability. Brown holds a narrow statewide advantage over Republican Senator Jon Husted, leaving turnout capable of deciding the November 3 special election. Younger voters could shape both the contest and which party wins the seat vacated by Vice President JD Vance. Preference alone does not win elections. Brown must convert support from a group with historically lower participation into votes while Husted works to offset the Democrat’s advantage elsewhere. Newsweek contacted Brown’s campaign for comment via email. Husted’s campaign told Newsweek via email that it did not comment on public polling. Key Points Brown Takes His Message to Students Brown brought his campaign to Ohio State University this week, speaking with more than 60 students about tuition, housing, employment, climate, voting rights and everyday expenses before casting an early ballot in Franklin County. “I was at Ohio State yesterday. Students are unhappy about costs,” Brown told reporters Tuesday. “When they graduate, they want a chance to get ahead, and they don’t see that opportunity they saw a generation ago.” The visit demonstrated an active effort to mobilize a constituency that appears receptive to his candidacy. It also placed affordability at the center of his appeal to people entering adulthood amid concerns about education, work and homeownership. Polls Show Generational Divide The age split is clear in the Times/Siena poll. Brown received 66 percent among likely voters aged 18 to 29, compared with 32 percent for Husted. Among those aged 30 to 44, the contest stood at 49 percent to 41 percent. That advantage reversed among respondents aged 45 to 64, who favored Husted by 51 percent to 43 percent. Voters aged 65 and older divided evenly at 49 percent apiece. The statewide survey of 616 likely voters was conducted September 22-October 1 and gave Brown a 3-point edge, 49 percent to 46 percent, meaning his lead fell within the Ohio subsample’s margin of error of plus or minus 4.5 percentage points. Separate research reinforces the pattern. Rasmussen Reports found Brown ahead 49 percent to 34 percent among Ohio voters under 30. That survey comprised 1,115 likely voters and was conducted September 22-23, with a plus or minus 3 percentage point margin of error at the 95 percent confidence level. A Quantus Insights survey produced a 51 percent to 31 percent split within that age group and put Brown up 50 percent to 39 percent among voters aged 30 to 44. The poll surveyed 695 likely voters September 21-23, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.2 percentage points. Its methodology report, however, cautioned that uncertainty was greater within subgroups. Enthusiasm Complicates Picture Those substantial margins carry a warning. “As expected, this race is narrowing,” Towery said after his InsiderAdvantage poll put Brown at 44 percent and Husted at 43 percent. “Brown continues to have a lead among younger voters, but they indicate a lack of enthusiasm about voting.” The pollster said adjusting the survey’s weighting to account for motivation could place Husted ahead. However, Towery also said that Republican enthusiasm trailed Democratic enthusiasm by 10 points overall, giving the incumbent a mobilization challenge of his own. Democrats Cannot Take Young Voters for Granted National history shows why campaigns distinguish between support and participation. CIRCLE at Tufts University estimated that 47 percent of eligible Americans aged 18 to 29 voted in the 2024 presidential election, down from 50 percent in 2020. Participation fell to 41 percent among 18- and 19-year-olds. The Democratic advantage within the group also narrowed dramatically. Young people backed Kamala Harris over President Donald Trump by 51 percent to 47 percent, following a 25-point preference for the Democratic ticket four years earlier. That experience makes Brown’s campus outreach strategically understandable without guaranteeing its effectiveness. Younger Ohioans may be among Brown's most favorable constituencies, but favorable polling cannot substitute for participation. Why Ohio Race Matters in 2026 Midterms Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority, counting two independents who caucus with Democrats. Democrats need a net gain of four seats for outright control because Vance would break a 50-50 tie in Republicans’ favor. That makes Ohio a valuable pickup opportunity among the 22 Republican-held seats being contested in 2026. A Brown victory would move Democrats a quarter of the way toward the four-seat gain they need; a Husted win would compel them to replace Ohio with another Republican-held target. Data Centers Become Election Flash Point AI data centers have become a dividing line in the Ohio race. Brown has attacked Husted’s past support for the industry and argued that large technology companies are driving up utility bills. Husted, meanwhile, introduced the Ratepayer Protection Act, which sought to prevent consumers from bearing data centers’ infrastructure costs, but it failed in the Senate after Democrats argued that it was too weak. Newsweek’s AI Policy Scorecard rates Husted as having a “mixed” position on AI, based on lawmakers’ voting records and public positions across areas including regulation, energy, employment, privacy and national security. Close Race Leaves Little Margin for Error Recent statewide surveys continue to show a competitive contest. A CNN/SSRS poll conducted September 29-October 5 placed Brown 6 points ahead, while Marist found an 8-point advantage among registered voters in late September. The CNN/SSRS survey questioned 760 likely voters September 29-October 5 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.5 percentage points. Marist surveyed 1,298 registered voters September 24-27, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points. RealClearPolitics classified the race as a toss-up and calculated a 3.2-point average lead for Brown using surveys conducted through October 1. Differences in samples, methods and margins of error prevent any single result from settling the contest. For Brown, the remaining task is therefore more practical than persuasive: ensuring that the young Ohioans telling pollsters that they prefer him actually cast a ballot. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Sam Stevenson and Dave Siminoff.
news.summary: Young Ohioans strongly favor Brown, but lagging enthusiasm could decide whether that support translates into votes in November.
news.author: Sam Stevenson

news.title: Jon Ossoff Enters Midterms Stronger Than His 2020 Breakthrough
news.text: Six years ago, Jon Ossoff reached Election Day as a young Democratic challenger trying to dislodge a sitting Republican senator in a state his party had only just begun to crack. He lost the first round. In November 2020, David Perdue took 49.73 percent of the vote, ahead of Ossoff’s 47.95 percent. Georgia’s majority requirement kept Perdue from winning outright and sent the race to a January runoff, where Ossoff reversed the result by little more than 1 percentage point. These days, the landscape greeting Ossoff in the upcoming 2026 midterms looks considerably different. He is now the incumbent, backed by one of the country's largest campaign accounts, and leads Republican candidate Mike Collins in every poll in the latest RealClearPolling average. That average, covering surveys conducted between September 10 and 23, puts Ossoff at 51 percent and Collins at 43.2 percent. The two candidates will meet for a televised debate Thursday at 7 p.m., with Georgia’s early voting period beginning less than a week away on October 13. Newsweek reached out to the Ossoff and Collins campaigns via email for comment. Political analyst Michael Fahey described the change since 2020 as “almost a different race.” “In 2020, Ossoff was the challenger trying to convince Georgia voters to take a chance on him,” Fahey told Newsweek. “Today, he’s the incumbent with six years to point to, a massive campaign operation and a political environment that, at least right now, is breaking his way.” From Runoff Upset to Incumbency In 2020, Ossoff’s path to the Senate left little margin for error: Perdue received 2.46 million votes in the November election, nearly 88,000 more than Ossoff. The Democrat then won the January 5 runoff by 54,944 votes, taking 50.61 percent to Perdue’s 49.39 percent. Ossoff is now starting from a different place. The six most recent surveys in the RealClearPolling average give him leads of 4 to 10 points, though two put him at 49 percent, an important distinction in a state where a candidate needs a majority to avoid a runoff. Polling a month before an election, as ever, remains only a snapshot of what could later materialize, predating the final weeks of campaigning, when candidates make a last-ditch effort to drum up support. Still, Ossoff spent much of his 2020 campaign trying to catch up to an incumbent who ultimately finished ahead of him in the first round. While he eventually prevailed, Ossoff has several advantages this time around that weren't available to him in 2020. “The biggest difference is that voters don’t have to imagine what Senator Jon Ossoff would look like anymore. They’ve seen it,” Fahey said. “That changes the burden of proof.” Kemp’s Absence Changed the Republican Field Perhaps one of the biggest boons to Ossoff's campaign is that the Republican who once seemed best equipped to beat him never entered the race. An Atlanta Journal-Constitution poll released in May 2025 put Republican Governor Brian Kemp at 49 percent against Ossoff’s 46 percent. Kemp was also the only Republican tested in that poll who came close to Ossoff, and his approval rating stood at 60 percent. But despite Republican leaders spending months encouraging him to run, Kemp announced days later that he would sit it out, saying a Senate campaign was not the right move for him or his family. “Kemp not running was enormous,” Fahey said. “If Republicans could have designed the ideal candidate to challenge Ossoff, Brian Kemp would have been very close to it. He had already won statewide, had his own political identity separate from Donald Trump, and could compete for exactly the suburban and independent voters Republicans need to get back. His decision took arguably the GOP’s strongest possible option off the board." Daniel Schatz, a political scientist and former visiting scholar at Harvard, Stanford and Georgetown universities, described Kemp’s decision as “probably the single most consequential development in the race.” “He was the Republican most plausibly capable of combining the party’s base with enough crossover and suburban support to put Ossoff under real pressure,” Schatz told Newsweek. Collins brings a different political profile. The congressman won the Republican nomination after a June runoff and has Trump's backing. RealClearPolling currently rates the race as leaning Democratic, while its average places Collins in the low 40s. A Campaign Built to Spend Ossoff’s financial advantage in the 2026 election is difficult to miss. His campaign raised $77.3 million between the beginning of 2025 and June 30, according to the Federal Election Commission, while spending $39.7 million. It finished June with $42.6 million still in the bank. The FEC currently lists Ossoff among the leading fundraisers running for federal office in 2026. “Money doesn’t buy an election, but having tens of millions more than your opponent certainly buys options,” Fahey said. “Ossoff can advertise everywhere, organize everywhere and respond immediately when Collins attacks him.” Ossoff entered the final stretch of his 2020 general-election campaign with about $8.3 million cash on hand. By June 2026, his balance was more than five times that amount. As for Collins, his principal Senate committee raised about $6.5 million through the same date and held just over $2 million. His separate Republican nominee fund raised another roughly $897,000 and held about $42,000. “Ossoff’s cash advantage is not cosmetic,” Schatz said. “A large war chest buys early advertising, field organisation, rapid response and the ability to define an opponent before outside groups do it for you. It does not guarantee victory—Georgia remains a closely divided state and Republican super PACs can narrow the gap—but it gives Ossoff greater control over the campaign’s message and tempo.” Republicans can narrow that funding disparity through outside spending. Senate Majority Leader John Thune campaigned with Collins in September and said the Senate Leadership Fund would continue directing resources toward Georgia. "It takes resources to compete in Georgia, no question about it," Thune said at the time. "It's an expensive state, especially in the Atlanta market, but we're doing everything we can to get those resources in this direction. And we believe that Mike Collins can win here." Jon Ossoff, the Senator Money talks, but it is only part of what six years in office has reaped for Ossoff. His reelection operation has leaned heavily on constituent service and local projects, including assistance after Hurricane Helene, infrastructure work, veterans’ issues, and meetings with unions. “For far too long, no matter which party has been in power, it’s been metro Atlanta and not smaller cities and rural parts of Georgia that have gotten the love and attention that you deserve, and Raphael and I together have worked to change that,” Ossoff said during his visit to Rome in northwest Georgia in July, referring to fellow Democratic Senator Raphael Warnock. “Incumbency matters when it is made tangible,” Schatz said. “Ossoff can point to constituent service, federal funding, disaster response and local issues in a way he could not as a challenger in 2020.” The approach has produced crossover support and a handful of Republican endorsements. Republican mayors Julie Smith of Tifton and Scott James Matheson of Valdosta have both endorsed him. Donald Chase, the Republican chair of the Georgia Peanut Commission who has voted for GOP candidates for most of his life, is also backing Ossoff while supporting Republicans elsewhere on the ballot. Blue vs. Red in Georgia Ossoff’s push beyond reliably Democratic territory matters because Georgia is, as is well known, one of the country's most finely balanced states. Democratic strength in Georgia is concentrated around metro Atlanta. Fulton, DeKalb and Clayton counties form the party’s strongest base, while Cobb and Gwinnett have moved sharply away from their Republican pasts over the past decade. Cobb, once a GOP stronghold associated with figures including former House Speaker Newt Gingrich, is now largely controlled by Democrats at the local level. Gwinnett has followed a similar trajectory: after decades of Republican dominance, Joe Biden won 58 percent of the county in 2020. Both counties stayed Democratic in 2024. Kamala Harris won 228,404 votes to Donald Trump’s 168,679 in Cobb and carried Gwinnett by about 16 points. However, things change beyond the Atlanta region, where Republicans dominate large parts of rural and exurban Georgia, while Democrats retain support in cities including Savannah and Athens and in several more Democratic counties elsewhere. Trump won all but 27 of Georgia's 159 counties in 2024 and improved his performance across much of the state. This time, Ossoff needs strong turnout in Atlanta and other Democratic areas, healthy margins in suburbs such as Cobb and Gwinnett, and enough support elsewhere to keep Republicans from edging into his vote share. Washington Offers a Boon Ossoff, like many of his fellow Democratic candidates, may well benefit from the current administration on his path to a second Senate residency. Nationwide, the midterms are hardly ever a resounding success for the president’s party. From 1934 through 2022, the president’s party lost an average of 27 House seats and three Senate seats in midterm elections. It lost seats in both chambers in roughly two-thirds of those elections, according to the American Presidency Project. “Midterms often become a referendum on the White House, and if voters remain dissatisfied with the economy, prices or the administration’s broader direction, that creates a favourable backdrop for Democrats,” Schatz said. Trump’s approval rating stood at 32 percent in an October Reuters/Ipsos poll, while Democrats led Republicans 44 percent to 37 percent among registered voters surveyed about the congressional election. Some Republican candidates in competitive races have created distance from parts of Trump’s agenda to help their own campaigns. “Georgia may have its own political personality, but it is not immune from national gravity,” Fahey said. “Midterms are usually a referendum on the party controlling Washington, and right now that works to Ossoff’s advantage. Republicans are dealing with an unpopular Republican president and a national environment that has become increasingly difficult for their candidates.” Can The Race Still Move? Trump carried the state in 2024 after former President Joe Biden’s narrow victory four years earlier. Ossoff is the only Democratic Senate incumbent running this year in a state Trump carried in the last presidential election. His 2021 runoff also showed how demanding the Democratic turnout operation can be. Ossoff’s original Senate campaign banked on high turnout in metro Atlanta after the presidential election, while maintaining enough support elsewhere to overcome Republican margins across much of the state. If Ossoff can generate similar turnout and enthusiasm this year, his current polling advantage may well hold through to Election Day. But as is often the case in politics, opponent Collins could still benefit from an influx of national Republican money, gains among suburban voters or an unforeseen change in the local and national political atmosphere. The Final Stretch Georgia’s early voting period runs from October 13 through October 30, followed by Election Day on November 3. A December 1 runoff awaits if neither Ossoff nor Collins achieves more than 50 percent of the vote. For now, Ossoff's current polling average sits at 51 percent, although individual surveys have placed him just below the threshold. The next three weeks will put his accumulated advantages to the final test: an enormous campaign account, six years of incumbency, strong Democratic territory around Atlanta and an effort to build support beyond it. “The greatest risk for Ossoff is complacency,” Schatz said. “His current position is strong, but the race could tighten quickly if national Republicans fully concentrate their financial firepower on Georgia, if Collins improves his standing with suburban voters, or if the national political environment changes. Ossoff needs to retain his fundraising edge, keep his campaign locally focused and ensure Democratic turnout resembles 2020 rather than a traditional midterm drop-off.” Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Ben Kelly and Sam Wilson.
news.summary: Jon Ossoff is making his bid to retain his Georgia Senate seat with a clear advantage.

news.title: Abdul El-Sayed’s long history of trashing Obama resurfaces ahead of rally with former prez
news.text:
WASHINGTON — Democratic Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed repeatedly rebuked former President Barack Obama as insufficiently progressive in writings and comments that have resurfaced ahead of a high-profile rally featuring the two men later this month.

“I have to say now what I’ve been holding in throughout his campaign, and what I think all of us have to admit: Obama was not the right choice — he just wasn’t the wrong one,” El-Sayed wrote in a 2012 HuffPost piece right after Obama’s re-election victory.

“This leader has perpetuated war, violated our civil liberties, deported more people from our shores than any other president before him, and the list of his failures goes on.”

On the campaign trail, El-Sayed has recounted the excitement he felt when Obama won the presidency in 2008.

“In 2008, a guy named Barack Hussein Obama runs for and wins the presidency. I got to be honest with you all, it’s the first time I ever saw myself reflected in politics at all,” El-Sayed, 41, said at an August rally.

But in the 2012 op-ed, El-Sayed repudiated his feelings of four years earlier.

“The jubilation of his 2008 election will forever live with me,” he wrote. “But for me, that memory will serve not as a reminder of the history we made that night — but of the silly emotions of a naïve young man who didn’t understand that hope and change required more than flowery prose and a winning smile.”

The future candidate went on to assert that the US was not “better off” under Obama and trashed the 44th president’s signature Affordable Care Act as “watered-down reform that kowtows to the interests of healthcare lobbies.”

El-Sayed’s critiques of Obama continued even after the first black president left office, according to a chronology by CNN.

During his unsuccessful Michigan gubernatorial bid in 2017, El-Sayed gave an interview with Vox in which he attacked Obama for his “fairly centrist, middle-of-the-road Democratic policies.” The resulting piece was titled “Don’t Call This Man ‘The Next Obama.”

Three years later, in January 2020, El-Sayed warned Democrats at a University of Chicago Institute of Politics panel against repeating “the same mistakes of the past eight years under Barack Obama.”

“We are not, as a country, better off eight years after Obama was elected in 2008 than we were when he was elected. And I say this as somebody who loves him deeply,” he said.

“I appreciate the fact that we don’t give him credit for what he did for the economy in the short term. But the structure of the economy did not change under Barack Obama,” added El-Sayed, arguing the Democrat’s shortcomings set the stage for President Trump’s rise.

“At 24, I watched President Obama win in 2008,” El-Sayed told CNN in a statement. “He changed what was possible for someone like me, with a name like mine. Despite being dealt one of the toughest hands of any American president—he handled it.

“And despite all he did, there remains so much left to do. That’s where the next generation, inspired by him and his leadership, picks up. We stand on the shoulders of giants—and I can’t wait to tell him myself later this month.”

El-Sayed is locked in a tight race against Republican former congressman Mike Rogers and has been criticized by both Jewish and black groups for his near-obsessive focus on the Middle East and Israel’s war against Hamas in the Gaza Strip.

Last month, he stumped with former Vice President Kamala Harris, despite El-Sayed backing the 2024 “Uncommitted” movement — which refused to endorse Harris against Trump in the crucial state.

El-Sayed’s campaign and representatives for Obama did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The pair are scheduled to appear together and alongside other Michigan Democratic candidates Oct. 24 in Detroit.
news.summary: Dr. Abdul El-Sayed is set to embrace former President Barack Obama, a man he once excoriated as a failure who perpetuated war and undermined liberty, newly resurfaced past commentary has revealed.

news.title: Pennsylvania Gov. Shapiro, challenger Garrity remain aligned on Israel in midterm debate
news.text: Democratic Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and GOP opponent Stacy Garrity faced off on Wednesday in a heated gubernatorial debate, clashing over most policy issues - with the notable exception of Israel. “I want to recognize the anniversary of the Hamas attacks, where 1,200 innocent people were killed, including 49 Americans,” said Garrity, referring to the third anniversary of Hamas' October 7, 2023, attack on Israel. “I want to remember the lives that were stolen, the families that were changed forever, and the Americans that didn't make it home,” she added. While Garrity, Pennsylvania's state treasurer, has the endorsement of US President Donald Trump, Shapiro leads by 25 percentage points in a poll released Wednesday. Both candidates won their primaries uncontested in May, and both have been outspoken against antisemitism. Shapiro, who himself is Jewish, likewise recognized “the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre” at the debate. He recalled how “Hamas, a terrorist organization, broke into Israel and murdered 1,200 innocents, took over 250 hostage, including many Americans.”“This is a moment where my heart stands with the people of Israel,” he said. “My heart stands with the Jewish community, who I know are grieving as a result of this.”“This is a moment where we need to stand together against terrorism, against hate and against antisemitism,” the governor added.Shapiro, Garrity clash on death penalty, tariffs, voter ID, taxesAlthough the candidates shared similar perspectives on Israel during Wednesday's debate, they clashed on numerous other topics, including the death penalty, voter identification, taxes, and tariffs.Asked by the debate moderator about the plunging support for Israel in the Democratic Party, Shapiro replied that he has “been very, very consistent” in both his “love of Israel” and his disagreements with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Shapiro then noted that Israelis will head to the polls in just a few weeks to choose their next leader. He expressed hope that they would not elect Netanyahu, whom he said “has led Israel down a very dangerous and isolated path.” “I want America to have a strong relationship with Israel and with the Israeli government,” Shapiro added. “That's not possible right now with the Netanyahu government in charge.”Shapiro seen as presidential hopeful for 2028Shapiro, one of the most prominent Jewish Democrats nationwide, was among the final candidates Kamala Harris considered in her vice-presidential search for the 2024 election. He is also seen as a possible 2028 presidential hopeful. But Shapiro has also faced the challenges posed by increasing antisemitism in America. During Harris's search, for example, a website and social media feed labeled him “No Genocide Josh” over his support for Israel. In April 2025, an arsonist set fire to Shapiro's house just hours after his family had conducted a Passover seder. In 2018, while Shapiro was serving as Pennsylvania's attorney general, a terrorist killed 11 people and injured six others at the Tree of Life synagogue in Pittsburgh.Garrity, meanwhile, has more than tripled Pennsylvania's investment in Israel bonds in her current role. She invested $20 million after the October 7 attack and another $35 million in July 2025.

news.title: New Poll Sounds Pretty Ominous Alarm For Republicans Ahead Of Midterms
news.text:
Oct 8 (Reuters) - Voters who backed Democratic former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024 are far more enthusiastic about casting ballots this November than those who supported President Donald Trump, a Reuters/Ipsos poll found, in a potential warning sign for Republicans heading into the midterm elections.

The six-day poll, completed Monday, also found that men were more enthusiastic about voting and more certain to cast ballots than women, and that male voters showed signs of shifting toward Democrats.

That could signal erosion in Republican support among a demographic that was a pillar of Trump’s 2024 victory.

Some 48% of 2024 Harris voters said they were “very enthusiastic” about voting in the November 3 midterm elections, when control of both chambers of Congress is at stake. By comparison, just 30% of Trump voters said the same in the poll.

The findings add to evidence of an enthusiasm gap favoring Democrats and suggest potential cracks in the coalition that propelled Trump in 2024, when he won the popular vote. That coalition was fueled by strong support from men and gains among Hispanic voters and other demographic groups that shifted to the right in the 2024 election.

The poll also adds to a string of encouraging signs for Democrats, who are widely favored to win control of the House of Representatives and remain competitive in the fight for the Senate as Trump’s approval ratings have slipped amid voter concerns about the cost of living and the war with Iran.

Republican strategist Charlie Gerow said the poll’s findings raise the stakes for his party’s turnout efforts, though he expects the enthusiasm gap to narrow as concerns about what he described as far-left Democrats gaining power motivate Republican voters.

“The enthusiasm has to be ginned up among Republicans because turnout is what’s going to determine the outcome of these midterm elections,” Gerow said.

While Trump voters overwhelmingly plan to vote Republican and Harris voters are similarly inclined to vote Democratic, the president’s 2024 supporters are less decided, with 13% saying they aren’t sure who to vote for in congressional elections, compared to 7% of Harris supporters who say the same.

BROAD DECLINE IN SUPPORT

The poll, which was conducted nationwide and surveyed 4,506 adults online, showed that just 32% of Americans approved of Trump’s presidency, holding at a record low first marked in a September Reuters/Ipsos survey. The survey has a 2 percentage point margin of error.

Since taking office in January 2025, support for Trump has fallen across every major demographic group, including double-digit drops among Hispanics, men, rural and suburban voters, people without college degrees and evangelical Christians.

One notable shift has come among men, a group Trump won in all three of his presidential campaigns, including by a 12-point margin in 2024, according to a Pew Research analysis.

When asked how they would vote in a congressional race if the elections were today, men in the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll picked Democrats over Republicans, 43% to 39%. The four-point Democratic advantage was the widest of Trump’s second term. Men consistently favored Republicans in 2025 but since August have mostly favored Democrats.

The warning signs for Republicans reflect growing voter concerns about the high cost of living amid a surge in gasoline and diesel prices following the war with Iran. Trump launched the Iran attacks in February, despite pledging during his campaign not to start new conflicts and to lower costs for consumers.

Cost of living is the top issue on Americans’ minds as they decide how they will vote next month, the Reuters/Ipsos poll found. Voters cite democratic values as the second biggest issue, followed by immigration.

Republicans continue to hold an edge among older voters, a crucial bloc in midterm elections, when seniors have historically accounted for an outsized share of the electorate.

Voters 50 and older still favor the Republican Party over the Democratic Party by 2 percentage points, 44% to 42%, though that was down from an 8-point Republican advantage in December.

Still, the enthusiasm gap looms large for Republicans.

Among all the voters in the poll who said they were enthusiastic, 62% said they were pumped about expressing opposition to Trump, compared to 36% who said they were eager to support the president.

Linda Rivera, a 46-year-old Trump voter in Pennsylvania, said that while she would probably vote Republican if she casts a ballot, she is frustrated with both parties and feels “neither enthusiastic or unenthusiastic” about voting next month.

Rivera, a respondent in the poll, said concerns about widespread voting fraud - which have been repeatedly fanned by Trump and his Republican allies without evidence - have added to her doubts about whether she will vote.

“I have lost faith in the voting process,” she told Reuters. “I have lost faith in both parties. Not just one.”

news.title: Sports media outlet considers Sophie Cunningham more polarizing than Megan Rapinoe
news.text: This week, a columnist for The New York Times’ The Athletic called for the Indiana Fever to part ways with Sophie Cunningham. "She’s too turbulent to be paired with Caitlin Clark," Candace Buckner wrote in the headline. "[I]f the Fever ever want to go back to being a basketball team again and follow the lead of rivals openly clashing with the forces trying to hijack their league, then Cunningham has to go," she added. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! The column portrays Cunningham as an outspoken agitator whose growing profile has become a distraction for the Fever. As evidence, Buckner cited comments Cunningham made earlier this year in an ESPN article about trans athletes competing against girls. For background, Cunningham said she "loves" all communities but believes it is important to "protect young girls" and that they "shouldn’t have to go against biological men" in sports. WNBA players and members of the media subsequently framed those comments as transphobic. We emphasize that particular comment because, beyond it, Cunningham has hardly been the political lightning rod her detractors depict her as. THE ATHLETIC COLUMN URGING INDIANA FEVER TO PART WAYS WITH SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM DRAWS WIDESPREAD CRITICISM Most of Cunningham’s public persona consists of playing basketball, dancing on TikTok, and trying on outfits. One could argue that her personality and attractive appearance have contributed to her supposed polarizing status. As Sydney Sweeney could attest, a certain corner of the media and social media seems uniquely irritated by attractive blonde women who refuse to apologize for it. The second-most controversial thing Cunningham has said recently was telling A’ja Wilson to "grow up" after Wilson charged toward a courtside fan who pointed at her during a playoff game. Teammates had to restrain Wilson before arena security intervened. And yet, The New York Times’ sports vertical has seen enough. It's time for the Fever to move on, the reporter declared. One might find The Athletic’s position more persuasive if it were consistent. But it's not. It never has been. Consider soccer player Megan Rapinoe. Unlike Cunningham, Rapinoe spent years making politics central to her public identity. She knelt during the national anthem and later said she would probably never sing it again. She claimed during the 2019 World Cup that she was "not going to the f---ing White House" if President Donald Trump invited the team. She publicly supported Democratic candidates, including Hillary Clinton and Elizabeth Warren. She described Trump as "sexist," "misogynistic," "small-minded," "racist," and "not a good person." Rapinoe also condemned the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision overturning Roe v. Wade as "sad and cruel," became a prominent supporter of Black Lives Matter, repeatedly advocated for transgender women to compete in women’s sports, and once dismissed concerns about competitive fairness as "total bullshit." More recently, she called for traditional WNBA media to make room for people who "understand queer culture." MEGAN RAPINOE SAYS WOMEN'S SPORTS ARE FACING 'REGRESSION' OF 'EQUAL RIGHTS' IN NEW KAMALA HARRIS INTERVIEW After tearing her Achilles in the final match of her career, Rapinoe said afterward that the injury was "proof that there isn’t" a God. Whatever one thinks of those positions, no reasonable person could describe Rapinoe as reluctant to inject politics, religion, and contentious social issues into sports. Yet the sports media never mounted a campaign for Rapinoe’s teams to part ways with her because she was too "turbulent." Her activism was not treated as an impediment to her team getting "back to being a soccer team." Quite the opposite. Rapinoe became one of the most celebrated athletes in American sports media, in no small part because of her willingness to speak about politics – the right side of politics, that is. Her activism was incorporated into her public brand and routinely presented as evidence of courage and leadership. That is the double standard. The sports media rarely treats athletes who espouse liberal or progressive political views as problematic, even when those views are provocative, divisive, or factually incorrect. The latter is quite common. Rapinoe is not the only example. LeBron James has spent years commenting on presidential politics, policing, and race all in favor of Democratic positions. Colin Kaepernick turned an anthem protest into the defining feature of his public identity. Sue Bird, Breanna Stewart and Natasha Cloud have routinely spoken about progressive political causes. Steve Kerr has addressed topics ranging from gun control to presidential politics and supported Kamala Harris for president on stage at the Democratic National Convention in 2024. news.title: First debate with Mike Rogers will be a key test for Abdul El-Sayed
news.text:
Michigan’s first U.S. Senate debate Oct. 8 will serve as a major test for Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed as he seeks to unify his party and prove that a progressive can win a battleground state. 

El-Sayed will face off against former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers, who has sought to paint the former Wayne County health director as too far-left.

El-Sayed has tied Rogers to unpopular policies from President Donald Trump’s administration, including a trade war with Canada, Michigan’s biggest export partner, and higher costs resulting from the war in Iran. 

The debate comes as national Democrats have raced to bolster El-Sayed after his narrow victory in an August primary against the more moderate Rep. Haley Stevens. Former Vice President Kamala Harris endorsed and campaigned with El-Sayed in Detroit Sept. 22 and former President Barack Obama will rally with the Senate candidate and Democrats’ gubernatorial nominee, Jocelyn Benson, on Oct. 24. 

But El-Sayed has also faced resistance from pockets of the Democratic coalition, including Jewish voters wary of his staunch criticism of Israel and moderates who don't support progressive policies such as Medicare for All. His campaign has also sought to consolidate his support among Black voters, who favored Stevens in the primary in polls. Those weak spots have created an opening for his GOP opponent, who has made direct appeals to those groups. 

The Michigan Senate race has taken on increased importance in the final weeks of the midterm election. While Democrats are running surprisingly competitive campaigns in Republican strongholds such as Kansas and Alaska, holding on to retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters' seat in Michigan is key to their hopes of flipping the Senate in November.

Recent polls show a close race. A Fox News survey released Sept. 30 found 50% of likely voters supported El-Sayed and 49% backed Rogers, within the margin of error. El-Sayed was backed by 77% of likely Black voters. (Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who narrowly beat Rogers in 2024, won 85% of the Black vote, according to CNN exit polls.)

The race could also have broader political implications for the Democratic Party, as El-Sayed’s campaign represents a rare opportunity for progressives to show their platform is viable even in more moderate parts of the country. Trump carried Michigan in 2024 by 1.4 percentage points.

“If Abdul can win in Michigan, anybody can win anywhere,” Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said at an Oct. 5 fundraiser for El-Sayed in New York, according to The New York Times.

Making the case on affordability

Both Senate candidates have spent the last weeks arguing that they’re the stronger pick to alleviate affordability concerns. 

El-Sayed previewed his responses to several of his critics' attacks during an Oct. 5 Fox News interview, in which he frequently referred back to higher costs. 

Asked about his relationship with Hasan Piker, the controversial Twitch streamer who campaigned for El-Sayed and other progressives during the primary season, El-Sayed said the race isn’t about a “streamer in California.”

“The reason I have a conversation with him is the same reason I have a conversation with you, because I want to talk to the folks out here who I want to have a conversation with,” El-Sayed said, referring to his decision to appear on Fox News. “Do you think that you’re better off now after two years of Donald Trump? Do you think that your gas is going to get any less expensive? Do you think that this war is justifiable or the tariffs in Canada?”

Rogers in recent days has sought to distance himself from those attacks. On Sept. 21 he released an ad, filmed in a grocery store, calling for a quick end to the war to bring down costs and urging a gas tax holiday. After previously defending the president’s tariff strategy, Rogers broke with Trump in an Oct. 7 ad calling for an end to the trade war with Canada. 

“Here in Michigan we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war now,” Rogers said in the spot, while holding a Canadian beer. 

Rogers has argued that progressive policies such as Medicare for All would be too costly, and has criticized El-Sayed’s past support for the Green New Deal, which he has argued would harm the state’s auto manufacturing industry.

An appeal to party unity

Part of El-Sayed’s challenge at the debate will be to assuage concerns from different factions of the Democratic Party.

Some of that work has already begun. El-Sayed’s appearance with Harris in September marked a turning of the page for the Michigan Democrat, who supported the Uncommitted Movement that protested the Biden administration’s approach to Israel. El-Sayed endorsed Harris the day after former President Joe Biden withdrew.

His past backing of the movement has raised concerns that he will underperform with Black voters, who may resent his reluctance to support the first Black woman to be nominated for president. 

El-Sayed must also strengthen his support among Jewish voters. Several prominent Jewish Michigan Democrats are backing the candidate, including Slotkin and Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel. And more than 850 Jewish voters and leaders in the state signed onto an open letter backing his campaign. But Republicans see an opening to win over some Jewish Democrats who disapprove of El-Sayed's criticisms of Israel. The Republican Jewish Coalition Victory Fund launched a $2 million ad campaign Oct. 7 in a bid to sway that bloc.

Adrian Hemond, a Democratic strategist based in Michigan, told USA TODAY he isn’t supporting El-Sayed because of the candidate’s stance on Israel and policies such as Medicare for All, which Hemond said would lead to tax increases on the middle class. But he said the key goal for El-Sayed ahead of the debate was to not stumble. 

“(El-Sayed) clearly has the momentum on his side — not because of anything that he’s doing, but because the president ran the economy into a ditch with tariffs and a war of choice in the Middle East,” Hemond said. “If Abdul doesn’t screw up, you have to call him the favorite in this race.”
