news.title: 'Blue tsunami?' Democrats expand midterm fight into deep-red states
news.text:
WASHINGTON — For one hour and 22 minutes, President Donald Trump plowed through his greatest hits, calling his opponents "sick individuals" who "hate America," declaring MAGA "the greatest political movement" in the nation's history and telling his followers "we gotta win" the midterm election.

But Trump wasn't speaking to a crowd in a traditional battleground state. He was addressing an arena full of cornhuskers in ruby-red Nebraska, which he carried in the 2024 presidential election by more than 20 percentage points.

"They're all saying we're in trouble in the midterms," Trump said in a meandering Oct. 5 speech as he campaigned with Republican Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts in Grand Island, Nebraska, warning that pieces of the MAGA agenda are at risk. "It could all be taken away if you start losing a couple of little elections."

Nebraska received little attention at the start of the midterm campaign cycle. Republicans expected to focus their efforts on states like Maine, North Carolina, Georgia, and Michigan. Polling over the summer moved Texas and Iowa into the toss-up category and landed with a shock.

But one month before the Nov. 3 election, Democrats are increasingly playing offense in historically Republican states and districts as the battleground map expands into even redder parts of the country: Alaska, Kansas, Nebraska, and even South Carolina.

It's the latest evidence that the expected blue wave could be even bigger than expected, and could not only give Democrats control of the House, but also the Senate, once thought to be a long shot.

Midterm elections: Trump takes extraordinary steps to target midterms, alarming critics

"This election has all the signs of a blue tsunami coming, and there's not really anything that the Republican Party can do to stop it," said David Cohen, a political science professor from the University of Akron.

Cohen compared the election outlook to the 2006 midterms, when Democrats flipped the House and Senate while George W. Bush was president. He said all the trends favor Democrats, including the presence of a deeply unpopular Republican president and hardened anxieties about the economy. He called Trump "an anchor for Republican candidates" and argued the president is making making matters worse by campaigning alongside them in their home states.

He also predicted Republicans' mid-decade congressional redistricting efforts, which added a number of GOP-leaning seats, won't be enough to stave off significant gains for Democrats.

"I mean, my gosh, we're talking about Democrats potentially winning seats in Alaska, and Iowa and Texas," Cohen said.

In the fight for the Senate, the dynamics have forced Trump and Republicans to spend valuable time and resources in Alaska, Texas, Iowa, and Ohio ‒ and more recently Nebraska, South Carolina and Kansas, each of which Trump won with double-digit margins in 2024. Polls show Democrats competitive or leading in each of these states, while also leading in the first-tier of battlegrounds such as Georgia, North Carolina and Michigan, and tied in Maine.

On the House side, where Democrats are now heavy favorites to take over, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee this week added six Republican-leaning seats to its midterm target list, including two seats Trump carried by more than 20 percentage points in 2024.

The political climate has also forced Republicans to begin making some tough choices on how to triage the expanding battleground map down the final stretch, including pulling money out of North Carolina, where the race to defend retiring GOP Sen. Thom Tillis's seat seems increasingly out of reach, while pouring funds into Kansas, where a Democrat hasn't won a Senate race since 1932.

The fresh signs of growing Democratic momentum come as Trump's approval rating is floundering at all-time lows, with Americans overwhelmingly opposing the U.S. war in Iran and blaming the president for high gas prices and their concerns over the economy.

"We win when they lose," said John Anzalone, a longtime Democratic pollster. "This was the guy who was supposed to fix the economy, and he's actually made it worse. His biggest strength has turned into his biggest weakness, and that's penetrated down to his candidates, who have followed along with him."

At the same time, the Democratic brand remains weak. Only 38% of Americans have a favorable opinion of the Democratic Party, about the same as when Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, according to a Wall Street Journal poll, conducted in September by Democratic pollster Hart Research and Republican pollster National Research Inc.

Though Republicans acknowledge several additional red states have turned competitive, they're banking on the party's significant financial advantage and Democrats' unpopularity to prevent a political earthquake. Trump and Republicans have worked to seize on the trend of far-left Democratic Socialists of America candidates winning primaries this cycle.

"There's no doubt that independent voters want to put a check on Donald Trump, but they also don't think that this Democratic Party ‒ with the DSA rising ‒ is worthy of putting in charge," said Republican strategist Brad Todd, partner of OnMessage Public Strategies.

A 'perfect storm' for Democrats in midterms

Republicans have been on the defensive in several solid red states and districts for months, but the emerging battlegrounds are a deeper shade of crimson.

The expanded map has opened new paths for Democrats to get the net gain of four seats they need to take over the Senate, where Republicans have a 53-47 seat advantage.

Among the Senate races that popped onto the national radar in recent weeks, Trump carried Kansas by 16 percentage points and South Carolina by 18 in 2024. Republicans are now ramping up spending in both states amid concerns that Democrats have momentum.

The six House districts Democrats recently added to their target list – spanning the map from Arkansas to Colorado, New York, Florida, Tennessee and Nevada ‒ went for Trump by an average of 16 points.

Trump's recent travel schedule reflects the GOP's need to protect home turf. In addition to deep red Nebraska, he has visited Ohio, Oklahoma, Alabama, and Texas (twice) over the last week, all states he carried handily.

He said he also plans to travel to Alaska to stump for Sen. Dan Sullivan, who is in a tough election against Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman.

Sean Spicer, who served as White House press secretary during Trump’s first term, said it makes sense for Trump to "shore up places that are critical to maintaining the majority" and expand from there.

"I’d rather that we don’t have to go to Nebraska," Spicer added. "I’d rather we didn’t have to be in Alaska. But you know, it’s a midterm, there’s headwinds, gas prices are where they are."

Republicans are facing "a bit of a perfect storm" of challenging midterm conditions, said Mike DuHaime, a GOP strategist and former political director for the Republican National Committee. The fact that GOP candidates are now facing tough Senate races in Kansas and Nebraska is "an obvious warning sign" for the party, he said.

"The political wind is blowing very heavily for the Democrats," DuHaime said. 

In a year when affordability is top of mind for voters, the September Wall Street Journal poll, which surveyed 1,500 registered voters, found 68% of Americans believe the country is headed in the wrong direction; 65% rate the U.S. economy negatively; and 60% say Trump's policies have made the economy worse.

Despite Americans' pocketbook concerns, Trump has said the economy is the greatest in U.S. history and "the country has never done better." But he's suggested the White House has struggled selling his achievements.

"We're doing a great job in running the country, but we're not doing a good job of public relations," Trump said in an Oct. 1 speech in Durant, Oklahoma.

Why Republicans are struggling in the Great Plains

Among the factors contributing to tighter-than-expected races in some of the emerging Senate battlegrounds: Republicans are facing candidates with more centrist profiles and encountering growing pushback over some of Trump's recent policies, which have hit regions with large agriculture industries particularly hard.

"For a Democrat to win Kansas or Nebraska … you need a very good candidate on your side, you need a flawed candidate on the other side and then most importantly, you need the political environment to be in place," DuHaime said.

The Iran war has driven up the cost of fertilizer and diesel fuel for farm equipment, and the president’s trade fights also are weighing on rural communities in the Great Plains.

"The farm economy’s been hurt very badly," said Byron Dorgan, a former Democratic U.S. senator from North Dakota.

Rep. Don Bacon, R-Nebraska, who opted against reelection in November to retire, said the agriculture industry's struggles are giving the GOP "headwinds" in that region.

"You couple that with Trump throwing out verbal boomerangs every day, the headwinds get worse," Bacon, one of only three Republicans elected in districts carried by 2024 Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris, said.

Trump's second term: Republicans jump ship as Trump's anchor weighs heavy on party

Kansas is another state that was largely overlooked at the start of the campaign cycle, but is now among the most competitive Senate races in the country. Democrat Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor, is tied with Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, a physician, in the average of recent polls.

Hamilton has campaigned as a moderate and leaned on his faith. Marshall, meanwhile, has faced questions about suing his patients over unpaid medical bills. While Marshall has been a staunch Trump supporter, he recently distanced himself from the president in questioning immigration enforcement efforts in the state.

In Nebraska, Independent candidate Dan Osborn, a former union president, is trying to unseat Ricketts, while in South Carolina Republican nominee Darline Graham, the sister of late Sen. Lindsey Graham, faces Democratic physician Annie Andrews.

Trump has signaled concerns about both races. On the same day he campaigned with Ricketts in Nebraska, where a recent YouGov survey has Osborn leading, the president lashed out at Andrews on social media.

Axios reported Republicans are planning to spend $5 million in South Carolina to help Graham in the final stretch.

'Save as many seats as you can'

As Democrats expand the races they're targeting, the GOP has pulled back in contests that once seemed highly competitive.

Republicans once viewed North Carolina and Georgia as key pieces to their strategy to hold on to their Senate majority. But Senate Republicans' top Super PAC pulled its spending in North Carolina, according to ad tracking firm AdImpact, a sign they believe Democrat Roy Cooper's lead over Republican Michael Whatley is likely insurmountable. Democratic incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff remains comfortably ahead of Republican challenger Mike Collins in Georgia, according to recent polling.

DuHaime said it's smart to shift resources to more winnable races.

"It's frankly mature that they are recognizing it… the worst thing would be to ignore it," he said, adding it's smart to: "Face the triage, face it for real, save as many seats as you can. You know, this is a long game. There'll be another election in two years."

Texas, where Democrats have not won a Senate race since 1988, has become a money pit for the GOP and is increasingly looking like a must-win state for Republicans to stop a Democratic takeover. Outside Republican groups have poured $122 million into Texas to air ads slamming Democrat James Talarico and boosting Republican nominee Ken Paxton.

But even if Democrats again fall short in their decades-long quest to turn Texas blue, competitive races in other Republican-held states would leave the door open to a Senate takeover.

"America has become the battleground," Anzalone said, emphasizing Republican spending in states such as South Carolina, Kansas, Nebraska and Alaska. In the current political climate, he's convinced strong Democratic candidates running in some House districts Trump carried by 15 points have legitimate chances to win.

"We're in that territory," he said.

The GOP's hopes of blunting any potential blue wave rest on the party's cash advantage and ability to make Democratic candidates unpalatable to voters through a flood of negative campaign ads. Republican spending on ads for congressional campaigns outpaced Democrats by $200 million in September, according to ad-tracking firm AdImpact.

National Republican Congressional Committee spokesman Mike Marinella said Democrats are spreading themselves thin "pretending every district in America is suddenly a battleground."

"Democrats can put as many names on a list as they want, but they’re still begging for resources just to match Republicans’ air superiority while bailing out their radical socialist nominees," Marinella said.

Meanwhile, even as more red states have become competitive, Democrats are facing tough contests on more favorable political territory in Maine, New Hampshire and Michigan. That's given hope to Republicans that a blue wave isn't inevitable.

Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, is virtually tied with Democratic nominee Troy Jackson in a Real Clear Politics average of recent polls. Trump lost Maine by 7 percentage points in 2024, but Collins has worked to carve out an independent image and has won the seat five times before.

Democrats in Michigan, which Trump won by one percentage point, and New Hampshire, which Trump lost by 3, lead in the polls. But the races are closer than other traditional battlegrounds.

"We might get a lumpy election, where you have some odd results," said Todd, the GOP consultant. "I could easily see Republicans winning Senate races in Maine, New Hampshire and Michigan, and losing them in Kansas and Alaska. That'd be an odd election result, but it's entirely possible."

news.title: The Democrats are surging as the U.S. midterms near. Here's the data that has Trump's Republicans spooked
news.text:
The upcoming midterm elections are a crucial test for U.S. President Donald Trump and the party he's dominated for the past decade — and early data points suggest it could be something of a bloodbath for the Republicans come November.

Poll after poll released in recent days suggests the Democrats are poised to make major gains among voters who, only two years ago, would have never given the party a chance.

Large swaths of the American electorate appear to be souring on Trump, who returned to power promising lower prices and no more foreign wars — but instead delivered higher prices and a war on Iran in the first two years of his second mandate.

Inflation is also running hotter than it was in January 2025, when Trump's second term began — which is significant because his predecessor, Joe Biden, also presided over an era of higher consumer prices.

U.S. Federal Reserve raises interest rates for 1st time in 3 years

Researchers say Trump's tariffs have only worsened affordability; without them, prices might have actually fallen slightly, affirming what many economists long predicted.

Oil and diesel costs have spiked partly because of the war on Iran and the ongoing Russia-Ukraine conflict, the latter of which he promised to solve within 24 hours of taking office but has since struggled to help end.

After some early victories — stopping the surge of migrants with his border policies, and brokering peace deals — Trump's popularity has plummeted.

One number-cruncher says Trump is now the most unpopular Republican president since Herbert Hoover, whom historians generally regard as a failure given how he governed during the Great Depression.

"These are historically low approval ratings, like below Richard Nixon at the height of Watergate, and that really doesn't augur well for Trump and his party," said Asa McKercher, the Hudson Chair in Canada-U.S. Relations at the Brian Mulroney Institute of Government. 

"Not only is Trump unpopular, but so are his policies, which have not borne out … any fruit." 

That's why he is floating what McKercher calls "gimmicks" such as $5,000 cheques for every adult if the Republicans retain power in the midterms. 

"There's a sense of desperation there," McKercher said.

CBC ExplainsYour guide to the U.S. midterms, and why they're crucial for Donald Trump

Some Republicans distancing themselves

While Trump has repeatedly told his supporters to "pretend I'm on the ballot," thinking it will boost Republican fortunes in these congressional races, some of the party's candidates are distancing themselves given how toxic the president is in certain circles.

Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate candidate in Michigan, who closely aligned himself with Trump in the past, released a new campaign ad Wednesday denouncing the president's trade war with Canada.

Just this summer, Rogers said Canadians "have not been good partners," but that was before polling showed the vast majority of Americans are opposed to tariffs on their northern neighbour. Politico found only 26 per cent of Americans surveyed think the Canadian tariffs are the right thing to do.

Susan Collins, the Republican incumbent running in Maine's tight Senate race, has said something similar about tariffs, while strongly suggesting she doesn't want Trump to campaign in her state. 

"I’m not exactly his favourite senator," she said in a debate Tuesday.

More Americans now identify as Democrat

Perhaps the most revealing recent data point is the dramatic swing in how voters identify themselves when Gallup pollsters ask them to pick between the two parties.

For much of the last four years, Republicans held a clear edge.

Now, the Democrats hold a double-digit lead as some voters reject a party they thought would deliver better economic results, temper inflation and bring about peace.

Mark Bednar, a former spokesperson for House Speaker Kevin McCarthy who now works as a Republican strategist, said all is not lost for the party — Trump is still hugely popular among the MAGA base and he's defied the odds before.

But he said the party needs to urgently address what he calls the "enthusiasm gap," in which Democrats are much more motivated to turn out and vote than their Republican counterparts this year.

Will the U.S. midterm results affect Trump's tariffs on Canada? Democrats think yes

Bednar said there's one big bright spot for the Republicans that can help get those people fired up and off to the polls: a massive fundraising advantage.

Trump alone sits on a roughly $400-million campaign war chest that he can deploy in the closing weeks of this campaign to blanket the airwaves with ads and help boost candidates in tight races.

"The Republicans have a huge financial advantage and that gives them the opportunity to actually get out there, get your message on TV and tell your story as a Republican and prosecute the case against Democrats," Bednar told CBC News.

"The closer we get to these midterms, the closer the margins will be in some of these races."

Reliably 'red' states in play, polls suggest

These midterm elections will decide who controls the balance of power in Washington.

Despite state-level efforts by Republicans to gerrymander the maps in their favour, polls suggest the party is poised to lose the House of Representatives — the final result could be relatively lopsided even with the creative map-making — and possibly the Senate.

On the face of it, the electoral map this year looks unfavourable to the Democrats, with many contests in reliably Republican states. (Only one-third of Senate seats are up for election every two years.)

But the most recent New York Times-Siena poll, which politicos watch closely given its past accuracy, shows states long thought of as "red" ones are in play.

Kansas, for example, hasn't returned a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, but the Siena poll (and others) shows it could break that nearly century-old trend.

Farmers in particular have paid a dear price for Trump's trade war. Anyone who relies on a tractor or combine to get their products to market knows diesel prices have doubled on Trump's watch.

In the Republican crown jewel of Texas — where Trump beat Democratic nominee Kamala Harris in the last presidential election by nearly 14 percentage points — new Siena data shows Democrat James Talarico has a six-point lead over the embattled Republican Ken Paxton.

Polls reveal why there has been such a dramatic shift in that historically ruby-red state: Hispanic voters are turning away from the Republicans.

According to exit polls from the 2024 presidential election, 55 per cent of Hispanics in Texas voted for Trump. But just 34 per cent of Hispanics surveyed say they will back Paxton in this campaign, according to YouGov. 

About 64 per cent of Hispanics disapprove of the job Trump's done to this point.

This Hispanic shift follows nearly two years of immigration raids that rooted out many undocumented migrants, including some violent criminals, but also tore apart communities by removing people long established in the U.S.

But white voters in Texas, too, say they are much more likely to vote for Talarico, a political moderate and Presbyterian seminarian with a savvy social media presence, than they were for Harris two years ago.

The inflation-battered economy has scrambled the electoral equation elsewhere.

In Ohio, a "Rust Belt" state that voted for Trump by wide margins three times, Democrat Sherrod Brown is leading his Republican opponent by three percentage points in the Senate race. Brown's pitch: "Life is too expensive." 

As part of his recent campaign blitz, Trump visited both Ohio and Texas, but also Alabama and Oklahoma. This was an unusual move so close to a vote, when parties usually focus their leader's time on must-win swing states.

It suggests the definition of a "swing state" is much different now than in the recent past.

"This could be a perfect storm, where it's not just a blue wave but a blue tidal wave or tsunami for the Democrats," McKercher said.

About 64 per cent of Hispanics disapprove of the job Trump's done to this point.

This Hispanic shift follows nearly two years of immigration raids that rooted out many undocumented migrants, including some violent criminals, but also tore apart communities by removing people long established in the U.S.

But white voters in Texas, too, say they are much more likely to vote for Talarico, a political moderate and Presbyterian seminarian with a savvy social media presence, than they were for Harris two years ago.

The inflation-battered economy has scrambled the electoral equation elsewhere.

In Ohio, a "Rust Belt" state that voted for Trump by wide margins three times, Democrat Sherrod Brown is leading his Republican opponent by three percentage points in the Senate race. Brown's pitch: "Life is too expensive." 

As part of his recent campaign blitz, Trump visited both Ohio and Texas, but also Alabama and Oklahoma. This was an unusual move so close to a vote, when parties usually focus their leader's time on must-win swing states.

It suggests the definition of a "swing state" is much different now than in the recent past.

"This could be a perfect storm, where it's not just a blue wave but a blue tidal wave or tsunami for the Democrats," McKercher said.
news.summary: The upcoming midterm elections are a crucial test for U.S. President Donald Trump and the party he's dominated for the past decade — and early data points suggest it could be something of a bloodbath for the Republicans come November.

news.title: Trump makes late Nobel Prize pitch: ‘Not bragging ... but I settled eight wars’
news.text:
Donald Trump on Wednesday reiterated his call for the Nobel Prize committee to award him with its Peace Prize as he leaned back into talk of his peacemaking efforts.

Those peacemaking efforts, which he claims to tally at eight thus far, are ongoing, he says, and will soon include “another one” — even though there’s no sign yet of meaningful progress in talks between the U.S. and Iran regarding another ceasefire. Setting aside that it would come amid a war he himself started.

The president spoke to reporters at an announcement on his “Trump accounts” for children, after returning to Washington briefly amid his near rally-a-day spree of campaign appearances across the country.

“I’ve done stuff that nobody else has ever done. I’m not bragging, I’m just telling you the facts,” the president told reporters on Wednesday. “No president has probably ever settled any wars. I settled eight wars."

He then went after his first-term predecessor, President Barack Obama, whom he accused of not knowing why he’d received the 2009 Nobel Peace Prize. They gave the peace prize to Obama, then less than a year into his presidency, for his diplomatic efforts to reestablish ties with the Muslim world after nearly a decade of warfare in Iraq and Afghanistan led to a perception held by some that America was at war with the entire Muslim world.

The 47th president insisted on Wednesday that he was more deserving of the prize than Obama.

“Look, Obama got it, and he didn’t do anything-- he still doesn’t know what he got it for,” said Trump. “He got it when he was elected, right? Right at the beginning.”

“Whether I get it or not, I have done far more,” the president said.

The president frequently cites the “eight wars” statistic as a reference for his supposed peacemaking abilities, but the figure is not true. Several of the “wars” on Trump’s list were not wars at all, such as disagreements between Serbia and Kosovo which never escalated to real armed conflict during either of Trump’s two presidencies. Another one of the eight is the conflict between Iran and Israel, which very much remains ongoing as part of a three-way conflict also now involving the U.S. — that conflict has been ongoing for nearly eight months.

Still, the Iran war he unilaterally launched has largely shattered Trump’s image as a steward of global affairs, even in the minds of his own supporters, who embraced that depiction of the president during his 2024 campaign for a second term as he hammered Joe Biden and Kamala Harris over Israel’s relentless strikes against Gaza and the ongoing Russian invasion of Ukraine, both of which he pledged to end.

A year and a half after coming to power, Trump has made little to no progress in his efforts to negotiate an end to the war between Russia and Ukraine. A ceasefire exists in the Gaza Strip, where the majority of fighting has died down, but most Gazans remain in appalling conditions with much of the region’s infrastructure and housing destroyed. Israeli strikes continue to be carried out on camps of refugees, with continued civilian casualties.

The president’s touting of his diplomatic credentials also ignore one truth about his 2024 campaign: his promise to stop getting the U.S. into endless wars with murky objectives. His critics, both within and outside of the Republican Party, now accuse him of doing just that as the war in Iran has shifted from an effort to dislodge the Iranian government and take control of its remaining nuclear materials to ending disruptions over shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

Obama has long been a fixation of Trump’s, however, and the president attacks him nearly as frequently as he attacks Biden, who defeated him in the 2020 election. On Wednesday, he warned that his allies wanted to see the Justice Department wielded against Obama, Biden and Hillary Clinton, but claimed that he was respecting the sanctity of his office by declining.

"I could've done very bad things to Hillary Clinton. I could've done very very bad things to Joe Biden. I could've done very bad things to Barack Hussein Obama,” said Trump.

As he departed the White House for a campaign rally in San Antonio, Texas, the president reiterated his confusing claim that the war in Iran was already “won”, but not yet “over”.

“It's a war that's been won from the standpoint of what we have to do. We have to get rid of-- no nuclear weapons for, as you know, for Iran,” said the president. 

“We've taken away their nuclear power. If they would have had nuclear power, you would have had problems like you've never had before. So we did this for that reason. We've essentially accomplished that. Their military is now wiped out. Their whole country right now is wiped out. It'll be over very quickly. And when it does, and when it does, oil prices will come tumbling down.”
news.summary: Trump repeats claim that he has ended more than a half dozen conflicts while his administration has so far proved itself unable to reach a lasting ceasefire with Iran

news.title: The 2028 Race Is About to Start and JD Vance Has Already Won (Probably)
news.text:
We’ve still got the midterms to get through, so maybe it’s too early to talk about the 2028 presidential primary, but then again, why not? After all, the second that 2026 is decided, the 2028 cycle begins. It’s inevitable. Heck, it’s already happening. You can see politicians jostling for position, lofting trial balloons, and generally demonstrating how they are utterly overcome by delusion.

Here’s the fact: the nominee is going to be JD Vance unless either JD Vance or Donald Trump decides it’s not going to be JD Vance.

No debate. There’s no actual contest. That’s how it’s going to work out. That’s the only way it can work out. Anybody telling you anything else is wrong. They may be wrong because they’re crazy. They may be wrong because they’re dumb. They may be wrong because they’re delusional. Maybe they’re wrong and know they’re wrong but are saying it anyway because they think it’s to their advantage. But the truth is indisputable. Donald Trump is going to pick the next Republican nominee, and right now it’s JD Vance.

Now, of course, JD Vance might decide not to do it. He’s got a young and growing family, and his wife might not want to put up with this insanity. She might not want to live with a husband who is in the sights of every leftist sociopath out there with a gun and a grudge. They want to murder us, which we can tell by the fact that they have murdered us in the past and would’ve had a higher body count if they could shoot straight.

Alternatively, JD Vance might not think that 2028 is a great opportunity for Republicans. He’s young, and he’ll have many chances down the road, potentially. There’s always the chance that 2028 is his peak, and that somebody else will come along to grab the spotlight, but he might want to take a bye if things aren’t looking great and the administration is unpopular. But the thing is that things probably will look great.

Oh, if the Democrats take one or both houses of Congress, that’s going to be a mess, but that’s not going to reflect on Trump. That’s going to reflect on the Democrats. You’ll have a ravenous, roiling cauldron of left-wing insanity, weirdness, and perversion going on every single day, which will serve to remind people of what the alternative to sober, successful Republican rule is. In 2026, they’re doing everything they can not to remind people what they will do once they get power again. They won’t be able to hide it once they have a little; they’ve already promised to do nothing but investigate political enemies and try to impeach Trump. After the third, fourth, or even fifth impeachment, people are going to get a little tired of that nonsense. Political onanism only goes so far.

But the bigger problem for the Democrats is that Trump’s economy is going to start kicking in over the next year. The new golden age got delayed by trouble with the Fed and with the Iran war, but the economy is fundamentally sound and improving. Things are going to start rocking. We’ve seen this before, those of us who aren’t 12. Remember 1982? The great Ronald Reagan got crushed in the 1982 midterms because his economic policies hadn’t kicked in yet. But by 1984, they had, and it was morning in America, buddy. Reagan won every state except Minnesota, and the way Minnesota is going, that might be up for grabs in 2028, too.

Also, the Iran war is going to be finished by 2028, while Cuba’s going to be free; communists will be swinging from the lampposts — that’s Marco Rubio’s consolation prize for skipping the 2028 cycle. The problem for the Democrats is all they can do is stop legislation and complain. Trump’s going to get the credit for the economy, and the Democrats will have a track record of opposing everything that led to the golden age. And that means the next Republicans are going to have a solid opportunity in 2028, particularly if the Democrats nominate Kamala Harris, and what are the chances of them picking a creepy white sociopath like Gavin Newsom over a black communist woman?

I don’t think JD will let this opportunity go, and unless he gets in a big fight with Donald Trump — always a possibility — Donald Trump will anoint him, and most everyone in the GOP will fall in line.

But what about the guys who won’t? What about the guys who, despite JD's inevitability, throw their hat in the ring?

There would be two main kinds of competing primary opponents, the bitter and the delusional. Start with the bitter. These are the guys who’ve been rejected. These are the guys who’ve presented themselves to Republican voters and been soundly rejected. They’re terrible. They just don’t fit where we are, and it makes them mad that the peasants are revolting. How dare the proles not recognize their manifest superiority and entitlement to greater glory!

There are a bunch of these malcontents out there. I’m sure we’ll see Mike Pence give it another whirl; he’s the party guest who doesn’t know when to leave, except he doesn’t drink, so he didn’t even provide the entertainment that a drunk would. How about Don Bacon, that guy from Nebraska? He was an Air Force general, which says everything you need to know; rarely do you meet anyone else who is simultaneously so pleased with himself and so bereft of any reason to be a general officer jumping into politics. He’s pretty sure that the GOP needs amnesty and submission, but no one’s biting at that bait. That’s why he didn’t bother running again in his blue-leaning district; it wasn’t the Democrat votes he was worried about earning.

And then there are guys like Thomas Massie, the herpes of American politics — he’s gross and never goes away. He does speak for a constituency, though, the geniuses who are convinced there’s a giant Epstein conspiracy out there somewhere that Tommyboy will someday disclose — someday—and who also blame Jews for their inability to satisfy a woman. They are the perfect demographic for a cynical demagogue who does the impossible and makes libertarians look even more ridiculous.

Then there’s the delusional crew. These are good guys. They’ve come through for us in the past. They’d make good presidents. They’re just not going to make good presidents starting in January 2029, unless JD bows out for some reason, and Marco Rubio then bows out for some reason. That’s a lot of bowing, and it’s just not going to happen. I mean, it could happen. And they might come riding to the inauguration in a glittering silver carriage pulled by unicorns.

JD Vance is already taking some swipes at Ted Cruz and vice versa. I think Ted Cruz is a huge asset to the Republican Party. I did something for Ted Cruz that a guy like me — significantly Scottish — rarely does and gave him money the last time he ran for president, so I am speaking as a supporter. What I have to say as a supporter is this: Ted, buddy, you have zero chance of winning the nomination, so don’t waste our time and your dignity trying to win it in 2028. I know that Ted Cruz really, really wants to be president, and I think he’d make a good president, but over the next couple of cycles, a Ted Cruz presidency is the American political equivalent of “fetch.” It just ain’t going to happen.

John Kennedy is the senator from Louisiana who specializes in cornpone country-fried aphorisms and the surgical cross-examination of witnesses at committee hearings. Far from being some backward rube, this guy was a sensational trial lawyer (I read and appreciated his Louisiana Law Review pieces on products liability) and has made noises like he might give it a shot. OK, I like the guy. He’s doing a good job when he’s not going on weird, Trump-targeted tangents like pushing to outlaw naming buildings after living people five weeks before the midterms, but he doesn’t need to be president in 2028. Maybe somebody told him he’d have a shot, but he’s smart enough not to listen.

And there’s Brian Kemp from Georgia, who seems to think he’s got a shot. I don’t want to hear one damn thing about his presidential aspirations unless he delivers the governorship for Rick Jackson and the Senate seat for Mike Collins. And after that, I still don’t want to hear one damn thing about his presidential aspirations. He’s just not going to be president in 2028, and probably not ever.

Other good guys who get mentioned are Doug Burgum, Tom Cotton, Ron DeSantis, and several others. Again, all good guys. They all would make a terrific chief executive. But none of them is going to make a terrific chief executive next cycle. They should focus on doing the jobs that they’re doing. They can try again down the road.

With the emphasis on “down the road.” See, there’s a big roadblock in front of 2028. It’s Donald Trump, and he’s directing traffic on that figurative road. Right now, the only guy who’s driving through the barrier is JD Vance. You might not like it. You might not dig it. But that’s the way it is. And the sooner we all get that through our heads, the sooner we can start focusing on winning in 2028 — after we win in 2026, of course.

news.title: Obama hosts fundraiser with Senate Democrats weeks before midterms
news.text: Washington – Former President Barack Obama headlined a fundraiser for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Wednesday night to discuss the stakes of the upcoming midterm election.The event featured a conversation between Obama and Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, vice chair of the DSCC, about Democrats' efforts to flip the Senate. "I think he is just such a voice for our country, and of both realism and practical optimism, and I think we need that right now," Blunt Rochester told CBS News. "And I think he also lays the foundation for the significance of this election."Senate Democrats have become increasingly optimistic about their prospects this fall after several races shifted toward the party in recent weeks, including in deep-red states like Texas and Ohio that are considered toss-ups, according to CBS News' battleground tracker. "We do not want to be overconfident, but what we're seeing in state after state after state is that people are sick of Trump, they're sick of the Republican Senate going along with them, and they see the clear divisions we have drawn between what we stand for and what they stand for," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer told CBS News last month. "That has put us on the edge of victory." Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate. Democrats would need to pick up four seats to gain control of the upper chamber. Meanwhile, Republicans have argued they still have a path to hold on to the Senate."Right now, there's a lot of noise, there always is in the political atmosphere — some of it's created by our opponents," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a South Dakota Republican, told reporters before the body went on recess. "But if we can stay focused, talk about the future and the two paths over the course of the next several weeks, based on our record of accomplishment, things we got done, things we still need to do, we've got a great argument."One key target for both parties is Michigan. Democrats are trying to hold the seat being vacated by retiring Sen. Gary Peters while Republicans see it as a prime pickup opportunity. An exclusive CBS Detroit poll, conducted by Mitchell Research and Communications, shows Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed with a narrow advantage over GOP challenger and former Rep. Mike Rogers. Obama is expected to campaign with El-Sayed and other Democratic candidates in the Wolverine State later this month. A source familiar with the former president's thinking said his strategy this fall is "driven by where he can move the needle with Democrats and persuadable voters." The former president has also taped two dozen ads for Senate and gubernatorial candidates around the country. Last month, he participated in the second of two fundraisers with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, where he pressed Democrats to do more on the issue of artificial intelligence."Certainly if I were running for president next year, this would be one of my central agendas, and I would have a very clear plan, and I would talk about this, and I would say, 'Here's our plan for safety, here's our plan for making sure our kids are not corrupted by this,'" Obama said. "I would be thinking about the economic impacts in very concrete ways and understanding: What does it mean if there's going to be job displacement? Where is that going to hit? How are we going to respond?" Jeffries told CBS News he has remained in contact with Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris and expects both to be engaged through Election Day. The minority leader, who is poised to become the first Black House speaker if Democrats win control of the lower chamber, predicted that House Democrats would "take back the majority" this fall. "It's an all-hands-on-deck effort," Jeffries said.
news.summary: Former President Barack Obama headlined a fundraiser for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Wednesday night to discuss the stakes of the upcoming midterm election.

news.title: Tinubu’s extended absence
news.text:
NIGERIA has a disturbing habit of allowing those in power to treat constitutional restraints as inconveniences rather than obligations. Once again, the country is confronted with questions over presidential absence, constitutional compliance and the willingness of its institutions to hold the powerful to account.

At some point in September, President Bola Tinubu, Vice-President Kashim Shettima and Senate President Godswill Akpabio were all out of the country. That unusual coincidence alone should have triggered serious questions about constitutional responsibility and the functioning of government.

Instead, Nigerians were left with familiar explanations and little sense of urgency.

Tinubu embarked on a three-week European trip on August 30 and was expected to return on September 21. He did not. He extended his stay in France by another week, turning what was announced as a working vacation into a prolonged absence.

That immediately raises an important constitutional question: when a President is away for an extended period, what formal arrangements are made for the exercise of presidential authority?

The Presidency has previously argued that the President can perform his duties from anywhere in the world. That argument, however, does not answer the specific requirements of Section 145 of the 1999 Constitution.

Section 145(1) provides that whenever the President proceeds on vacation or is otherwise unable to discharge the functions of his office, he shall transmit a written declaration to the President of the Senate and the Speaker of the House of Representatives. Until he transmits a declaration to the contrary, the Vice-President is to perform the functions of President as Acting President.

That provision is not ornamental. It exists to guarantee continuity, certainty and constitutional order whenever the President is away or unable to perform his functions.

Nigeria has painfully experienced the consequences of ignoring that principle.

During the prolonged medical absence of the late President Umaru Yar’Adua in 2009 and 2010, power was not formally transferred to his deputy, Goodluck Jonathan. Then Attorney-General and Minister of Justice, Michael Aondoakaa, similarly argued that the President could perform his duties from anywhere in the world. That is blatantly absurd.

The result was a constitutional crisis that eventually forced the National Assembly to invoke the Doctrine of Necessity in February 2010, allowing Jonathan to assume the functions of Acting President.

The Buhari administration followed a similar pattern. In 2019, when President Muhammadu Buhari travelled to London on a “private visit” without formally transferring power to Vice-President Yemi Osinbajo, his spokesman, Garba Shehu, maintained that Buhari could exercise his authority from wherever he was.

Seven years later, Nigeria should not still be having this argument.

The Constitution provides a mechanism for dealing with presidential absence. Section 145(2) further provides for action by the National Assembly where a President fails to transmit the required declaration and remains away beyond the stipulated period.

The National Assembly therefore has a constitutional responsibility in such circumstances. It cannot simply look away because the occupant of the Presidency is politically powerful.

Unfortunately, Nigeria’s political class has repeatedly demonstrated an unhealthy reluctance to enforce constitutional restraints against those in power.

That is wrong.

A Constitution that is enforced only when convenient is not really a Constitution; it becomes a suggestion.

There is also the question of Section 143, which provides the constitutional procedure for the removal of a President or Vice-President for gross misconduct.

It should not be casually claimed that a presidential absence automatically amounts to an impeachable offence. But neither should the National Assembly behave as though constitutional breaches, where established, are beyond scrutiny.

The issue is accountability.

Presidents are not monarchs. They do not possess unlimited discretion. They hold office under a Constitution, and the powers they exercise belong to the Nigerian state, not to them personally.

That principle becomes even more important when presidential travel involves enormous public expenditure.

Why should a Nigerian President routinely spend extended periods on “working vacations” or “private visits” abroad when Nigeria has official facilities for presidential retreats and government work? 

What exactly is a “private visit” when the traveller is the President of Nigeria, accompanied by security personnel, officials and other members of the presidential entourage, with public resources inevitably involved?

Nigerians deserve answers.

Parking the presidential aircraft at a European airport for weeks does not come free. Neither do the security arrangements, logistics and other costs associated with maintaining the President and his entourage abroad.

This is happening in a country struggling to fund essential public services and where the government repeatedly pleads fiscal constraints.

There is nothing wrong with a President travelling. International diplomacy requires it. So do bilateral meetings, multilateral engagements and other legitimate state functions.

But a vacation is a different matter.

There is a reason responsible governments make clear arrangements for the temporary transfer of authority when their leaders are unavailable. Constitutional certainty is more important than personal convenience.

The United States provides a useful illustration. On November 19, 2021, President Joe Biden invoked Section 3 of the 25th Amendment to temporarily transfer presidential powers to Vice-President Kamala Harris while he underwent anaesthesia for a routine colonoscopy. Harris exercised the presidential powers for about 85 minutes before they were returned to Biden.

This demonstrates that constitutional clarity does not become less important because the period involved is short.

Nigeria should understand that lesson.

There have also been persistent public speculations about whether some of Tinubu’s foreign trips have had medical considerations. Such speculation should not be presented as fact without evidence. But neither can the Presidency reasonably expect Nigerians to ignore questions surrounding prolonged presidential absences.

The health and availability of a sitting President inevitably have a public dimension because the office carries enormous constitutional, security and economic responsibilities.

The Presidency therefore owes Nigerians clear and factual communication. Its media managers should stop treating legitimate questions as hostile attacks and start treating transparency as part of their responsibility to the public.

The taxpayers who finance the Presidency have a right to know why their President is away for extended periods, what official business is being conducted and what constitutional arrangements are in place.

More importantly, the National Assembly must remember that it is a constitutional institution, not an appendage of the executive.

Its members swear allegiance to the Constitution, not to the President.

If the National Assembly cannot insist on compliance when constitutional provisions are being tested by the executive, who will?

Nigeria has spent decades paying lip service to the rule of law while allowing political power to determine the practical limits of accountability.

That culture must change.

The President must respect the Constitution. The Vice-President must respect it. The National Assembly must enforce it. And the citizens must insist that they do.

Nigeria does not need more presidential explanations after the fact. It needs institutions strong enough to prevent constitutional ambiguity in the first place.

A President’s vacation cannot become a constitutional vacation.

No officeholder, however powerful, should be allowed to behave as though the Constitution is suspended whenever it becomes inconvenient.

Until Nigeria learns that lesson, democracy will remain less about the rule of law than about the discretion of those who happen to hold power.

A Punch editorial on President Tinubu’s extended absence, questioning the failure to transfer power to the VP as stipulated by the constitution.

news.title: Susan Collins' debate blunder baffles MS NOW's Nicolle Wallace: 'Ripe for SNL mockery'
news.text:
Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME) walked into a trap at her Senate debate with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson on Tuesday, bragging about how she got road salt exempted from President Donald Trump's tariffs on Canada, only for Jackson to point out that she's just chipping around the edges at a policy broadly hurting Maine and that "we can't eat road salt."

The moment left MS NOW's Nicolle Wallace astounded — and she was quick to analyze it alongside correspondent John Heilemann.

"I was a staffer, and so I'm sure a staffer was involved," said Wallace, noting that congressional staffers have had a bad couple of weeks with the Eric Schmitt incident. "This is a staffer who was told to go find something that Susan Collins was helpful with. And so someone said, I got one, I got one. They ... went to AI [and asked] 'Is there anything that we've made cheaper?' And they found one. They found road salt."

This was obviously going to backfire, said Wallace: "This is ripe for an SNL mockery. People are struggling to put gas in their car. Truckers are struggling to put diesel in their car. People are struggling to buy groceries. They were already more expensive in Maine. And you're going to tell people the road salt is cheaper. What?"

Heilemann agreed, calling it basic campaign malpractice.

"She slipped ... in terms of her political instincts," he said. 

Nor was it her only slip, said Heilemann, who noted that the defense of her vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh was also weak.

Despite all of this, he noted, the race remains highly close, at a moment when Democrats are polling better in red states like Alaska and Ohio. "It's closer than it would be, I think, if Troy Jackson had been the nominee throughout, if he had run in the primary," rather than replace scandal-plagued Graham Platner, he said. "He's the Kamala Harris of this race. He had to come in late."

news.title: Can $1 billion power Republicans to victory in the midterms?
news.text:
WASHINGTON — Republicans are entering the final month of the midterm campaign increasingly anxious that the $1 billion at their disposal may not be enough to fend off sweeping losses as the party reckons with President Donald Trump’s unpopularity, persistent cost concerns and the fallout from the war in Iran.

The cash advantage, spread out across a half-dozen groups, is driven largely by the Trump-aligned MAGA Inc., which had nearly $416 million in cash on hand at the end of August and began stepping up its spending on critical races in September.

But that money may have come too late, forcing the president’s group to pay much higher rates because of the shrinking availability of air time. Four Republican Senate campaign officials said groups that reserved advertising time last spring paid much lower rates than MAGA Inc. and its affiliated groups.

Instead, by waiting until September, Trump-connected organizations are sometimes paying more than five times what they would have spent if they acted earlier.

A representative of MAGA Inc. familiar with the group’s strategy said its spending has allowed Republicans to keep races more competitive than they would have been otherwise. In some cases, the group has been the only one on the air criticizing Democratic candidates.

The MAGA Inc. representative and the Republican Senate campaign officials spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal strategy.

The challenge is acute in places like Texas, where Trump will travel on Wednesday for the second time in a week to stump for Republican Ken Paxton’s Senate campaign. The state hasn’t elected a Democratic senator since 1988, yet MAGA Inc. has spent more than $22 million in the past month, according to the ad tracking firm AdImpact.

Another group, Texas PAC, which is aligned with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, has spent more than $83 million on advertising in the past month, an extraordinary amount to protect what’s normally a safe Republican seat.

One of those advertisements, which featured Paxton’s estranged wife saying she’s supporting the full Republican ticket, aired across the United States last weekend during a football game between the Dallas Cowboys and the Houston Texans.

Candidates are charged a lower advertising rate than outside groups, so the late infusion of super PAC cash has come at a steep price.

MAGA Inc., which is running ads primarily on streaming services, has been charged roughly $894 per airing, according to AdImpact, while Texas PAC has been charged roughly $809 for a mix of broadcast and streaming. That compares with about $290 for Democratic nominee James Talarico’s campaign, also on broadcast and streaming.

Those averages mask some of the more glaring disparities. For example, during a football game last month, Texas PAC was charged $450,000 to air a single spot in the Austin market. Talarico’s campaign paid $50,000 for a spot during the same game in the same market, according to AdImpact.

Elections are a referendum on the power of money

The 2026 campaign is shaping up as a referendum on the power of money in American politics. Democrats freely acknowledge their disadvantage, relying instead on anti-Trump sentiment among voters and targeted messaging on issues like corruption. Some Republicans, meanwhile, are open about the challenge of trying to spend their way out of a tough campaign at this late stage.

Neil Newhouse, a longtime Republican pollster, echoed concerns that his party was deploying its cash too late.

“After the votes are counted, I think we’re going to find the most effective advertising in terms of communicating message and moving voters and poll numbers, the most effective time was advertising that happened well before Labor Day, not after it,” he said. “A million dollars of advertising in October is a drop in the bucket.”

Thune’s group began pulling back in North Carolina last week, a sign of the party’s challenge in the Senate race there. The state’s outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis has been increasingly vocal about his party’s vulnerabilities and recently said that, even with a strong cash advantage, “in the last month, you pretty much have to place your bets.”

“If we have endless resources, then we should spend endlessly in every state,” he said. “Absent endless resources, you’ve got to make data-driven decisions about where you can win.”

The midterms mark the first national election since the Supreme Court in June erased limits on how much political parties can spend in coordination with candidates for Congress and president, injecting even more money into a political system already awash in cash.

Money alone doesn’t translate into victory

There’s plenty of evidence that money alone doesn’t translate into victory.

Democrat Kamala Harris entered the final stretch of the 2024 campaign with significantly more money than Trump but went on to lose every critical swing state and the White House. Elon Musk’s $25 million didn’t lift his preferred candidate to a Wisconsin Supreme Court seat last year. And Tom Steyer didn’t advance to the general election in the California governor’s race despite pumping $216 million of his own money into the campaign.

The $1 billion that Republicans have amassed compares with roughly $579 million held by a comparable collection of major Democratic groups.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said his party is facing an “obscene” amount of spending that could swamp them in the midterms.

“We’re never going to have as much money as them,” he said in an interview. “I sum up the election in this sentence: Can a massive Republican advantage in money beat a massive Democratic advantage in better candidates and political climate? I bet it can’t.”

In addition to Texas, Democrats have mounted competitive Senate campaigns in states like Ohio, Maine, Iowa and Michigan. A similar dynamic has emerged in governors’ races from Florida and Georgia to Wisconsin, Ohio and Nevada.

Former President Barack Obama is stepping up his involvement in the midterms and will headline a fundraiser for Senate candidates on Wednesday.

In the House, Democrats are growing so confident they can retake the majority that they’re expanding their targets deeper into traditionally Republican districts in Arkansas and Tennessee. But a lack of money could limit their gains.

“We absolutely need to spend enough to get our message out,” said Rep. Suzan DelBene of Washington, who chairs the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. “And district by district, we are.”

Trump turns to his bond with supporters

From his earliest days as an unlikely political figure, Trump has consistently overcome expectations. Facing daunting prospects heading into the final weeks of his last midterm, he’s betting he can again outwit political gravity, relying in large part on the deep bond he’s built with supporters.

He has stepped up his campaign rallies in recent weeks, traveling to deep red territory to galvanize the party faithful. At events like the one this past weekend in Vandalia, Ohio, the crowd was enthusiastic and cheered at the lines that have become Trump staples over the years, particularly when he dips into profanity. The high school gymnasium that held the event was packed, though crowds began emptying out about halfway through the 90-minute rally.

In the closing minutes of a speech Monday in Grand Island, Neb., the president revived his plea that supporters who have stood so fervently by him pretend as if he is on the ballot one more time.

“In a true way, I am running,” he said. “We have to keep it going.”

news.title: Trump says decided against prosecuting Obama, Biden, Clinton
news.text:
WASHINGTON, October 7. /TASS/. US leader Donald Trump said he could have pursued legal action against former US Presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama and former Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton but decided not to do so.

"I've had my shot and still do at Biden, at Hillary Clinton, and Barack Hussein Obama," Trump pointed out. "I could have done very, very bad things to Joe Biden. I could have done very bad things to Barack Hussein Obama. I thought it was inappropriate to do so because you have to treat the office of the presidency with respect," Trump told reporters. He is a Republican, while Obama, Biden and Clinton are Democrats.

Trump said people around him had urged him to pursue legal action against them. "I’ve had plenty of people say, ‘Let’s go get him,’ and I said, ‘No, you can’t do that to the presidency,’" he noted.

Trump won the US presidential election for a second time in November 2024, defeating Democratic candidate Kamala Harris. He previously served as president from 2017 to 2021 after defeating Clinton in the 2016 election.
news.summary: Trump said people around him had urged him to pursue legal action against them
