news.title: David Jolly Within Striking Distance of Byron Donalds: Florida Poll
news.text: Democrat David Jolly is trailing Republican Representative Byron Donalds by just 2 points in the race for Florida governor, according to a new YouGov poll, the latest sign that the contest to succeed Governor Ron DeSantis is tighter than many expected. The survey of 3,813 likely voters, conducted September 28 to October 5, found Donalds at 47 percent and Jolly at 45 percent, with 7 percent undecided. The gap falls within the poll's margin of error of plus or minus 2.7 percentage points. Newsweek reached out to both campaigns via email for comment. Florida has not elected a Democratic governor since Lawton Chiles won reelection in 1994, and Republicans have spent the past decade turning the onetime battleground into one of their most dependable states. President Donald Trump, who moved his legal residence from New York to his Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach during his first term, carried Florida by about 13 points in 2024. A close race for Trump's pick in his own home state would say a good deal about how much the national mood has moved before the November 3 midterms. What the YouGov Poll Shows The YouGov sample leans Republican by registration, 45 percent to 31 percent, and respondents said they backed Trump over Kamala Harris by 11 points in 2024. Even so, 54 percent of likely voters said they disapprove of the job Trump is doing as president, including 49 percent who strongly disapprove. Forty-six percent approve. Jolly's support is concentrated among younger voters. He leads Donalds 59 percent to 28 percent among voters ages 18 to 29 and 54 percent to 35 percent among those 30 to 44. Donalds leads 55 percent to 40 percent among voters 65 and older, who make up 39 percent of the poll's likely electorate. The poll also found Jolly ahead among Hispanic voters, 49 percent to 44 percent, a group that swung sharply toward Republicans in DeSantis' 2022 reelection and Trump's 2024 win. Donalds leads white voters without a college degree 59 percent to 33 percent, while white college graduates are nearly split, 47 percent for Donalds and 45 percent for Jolly. There is little crossover voting, and what exists favors the Democrat: 5 percent of Trump's 2024 voters back Jolly, against 1 percent of Harris voters who back Donalds. A Mixed Picture in Earlier Polling The broader picture is less settled. Some recent surveys show Jolly narrowly ahead, while others give Donalds a high single-digit or double-digit lead. Forecasters have steadily moved the race toward Democrats, but prediction markets still treat Donalds as a clear favorite. The other newest survey in the race came from Mason-Dixon Polling & Strategy. Its poll for NBC 6 Miami and Telemundo, taken September 28 to October 1 among 625 likely voters, had Donalds up 7 points, 48 percent to 41 percent. Two Change Research polls have pointed the other way. A survey for Freedom Project USA, conducted September 25 to 27, showed Jolly leading 48 percent to 46 percent, and an earlier September poll from the firm had him up 47 percent to 44 percent. A Hart Research survey for the Democratic Governors Association, released in late August, put Jolly at 46 percent and Donalds at 45 percent. Stetson University's Center for Public Opinion Research has the widest recent gap: Donalds 51 percent, Jolly 39 percent, in a survey taken September 14 to 21. The University of North Florida's July poll was tighter, with Donalds ahead 46 percent to 41 percent. Florida's recent history offers a caution for Democrats reading those numbers. In 2018, final polling averages showed Democrat Andrew Gillum ahead of DeSantis by several points, but DeSantis won by less than half a percentage point. In 2022, polls showed DeSantis leading Charlie Crist, another former Republican running as a Democrat, by low double digits, and he won by more than 19 points. Election forecasters have nonetheless shifted their ratings. The Cook Political Report moved the race from "Solid Republican" to "Likely Republican" in late August. Sabato's Crystal Ball, which rated the race "Safe Republican" until July, now has it at "Lean Republican." Decision Desk HQ went furthest, moving Florida from "Lean Republican" to "Toss-up." "Cook is saying the contest is no longer a complete lock," Craig Agranoff, a political professor at Florida Atlantic University, told Newsweek after the shift, "mainly because David Jolly is a former Republican with a ticket that can talk to independents." How Florida Became a Republican Stronghold Florida decided the 2000 presidential election by 537 votes and remained a perennial swing state through 2016. That changed quickly. Republicans overtook Democrats in voter registration in 2021, and the gap has since widened. As of June 30, the state had about 5.57 million registered Republicans, 4.04 million Democrats and 3.32 million voters with no party affiliation, according to the Florida Division of Elections. DeSantis' 2022 landslide, which included carrying heavily Hispanic Miami-Dade County, turned him into a national figure and briefly a rival to Trump for the party's 2024 nomination. Trump then won the state by double digits. Florida Republicans now hold every statewide office, and the state has become a pipeline for the administration: former Senator Marco Rubio left his seat to become secretary of state, and DeSantis appointed then-Attorney General Ashley Moody to replace him. The tension between Trump and DeSantis also shaped this year's primary. Trump endorsed Donalds early, while DeSantis stood behind Lieutenant Governor Jay Collins. Donalds won the August 18 primary with 47.8 percent of the vote. Donalds' campaign says it has raised more than $90 million, a financial edge that Jolly has not come close to matching. Ryan Smith, the campaign's chief strategist, dismissed the Sabato move in July. "Florida is a red state and will remain a red state in November when Byron Donalds is elected the next Governor," he said. Democrats See an Opening Democrats point to recent special elections as evidence that the state's rightward drift has stalled. In March, first-time candidate Emily Gregory flipped Florida House District 87, which includes Mar-a-Lago, defeating Trump-endorsed Republican Jon Maples. A Republican had carried the district by 19 points in 2024. Donalds had filmed an endorsement for Maples. Jolly, a former Republican congressman from Pinellas County who left the party during Trump's first term, has built his campaign around affordability, housing costs and opposition to new data centers. His running mate is former Democratic Representative Gwen Graham. "For the first time, the Florida governor's race is officially a toss up," Jolly wrote on social media after the Decision Desk HQ move. "Florida is winnable." "In this change election, Florida is ready to elect a Democrat," Mark Riddle, a senior adviser to Jolly, said in a statement. Donalds' camp has shrugged off the ratings changes. After the Cook move, communications director Gates McGavick posted "Nice try, guys" on X and said the campaign looked forward "to checking in with @CookPolitical on November 4th." Angie Nixon Faces a Steeper Climb in the Senate Race Florida's Senate race, a special election for the remainder of Rubio's term, looks somewhat less competitive. The YouGov poll found Moody leading Democrat Angie Nixon 49 percent to 44 percent, with 5 percent undecided after allocation. Both candidates' supporters appear locked in: 95 percent of Nixon voters and 94 percent of Moody voters said their minds are made up. Nixon, a state representative from Jacksonville and self-described democratic socialist, won the August primary with about 55 percent of the vote, defeating retired Army Lieutenant Colonel Alexander Vindman despite being outspent by roughly $17 million. Since the primary, the numbers have been all over the place. St. Pete Polls, surveying for Florida Politics, had Moody at 45.2 percent and Nixon at 44.8 percent. Change Research's poll for Freedom Project USA put Moody ahead by a single point, 48 to 47. Quantus Insights gave her a 7-point lead, and the July UNF survey had her up 8. Nixon has attacked Moody over a grand jury report that named the senator in a plan to steer $10 million from a Medicaid settlement to the Hope Florida Foundation, a nonprofit created by Florida first lady Casey DeSantis. Nixon called for Moody's resignation after the report's release. Moody remains a heavy favorite in prediction markets, which gave her a better than 90 percent chance of winning in late August. No Democrat has won a Senate race in Florida since Bill Nelson in 2012. Early voting begins later this month, and the election is November 3.
news.summary: Democrat David Jolly trails GOP nominee Byron Donalds by 2 points in Florida's governor race, a new poll finds.
news.author: Jesus Mesa

news.title: Gina Hinojosa Chance of Beating Greg Abbott Flips With Pollsters
news.text: As much of the attention in Texas this fall has focused on the U.S. Senate race between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton, another statewide contest has been tightening under the radar: Governor Greg Abbott's bid for a record fourth term. A new YouGov poll of 3,622 likely voters, conducted September 28 through October 5, has Democratic state Representative Gina Hinojosa narrowly ahead of Abbott, 48 percent to 47 percent, with 5 percent undecided. The margin of error is plus or minus 3 percentage points. Pollsters have traded leads all fall. A year ago, few Texas Republicans would have predicted that Abbott, who has won each of his three races for governor by double digits, would be scrapping for votes less than four weeks before Election Day. If Hinojosa wins, she would be the first Democrat to hold the office since Ann Richards left in 1995. If Abbott wins, he would be on track to become the longest-serving governor in Texas history. Newsweek reached out to Hinojosa and Abbott campaigns for comment Wednesday. Hinojosa Gets Strong Support From Black and Latino Voters Age is the sharpest dividing line in the YouGov survey. Hinojosa takes 64 percent of voters under 30 and 58 percent of those aged 30 to 44. Among Texans 65 and older, Abbott wins 61 percent to 36 percent. Gender splits the electorate almost evenly in both directions, with women backing Hinojosa 52 percent to 42 percent and men favoring Abbott by an identical margin. On race and ethnicity, Hinojosa leads Hispanic voters 58 percent to 37 percent and Black voters 80 percent to 12 percent. Abbott carries white voters by 21 points, a lead built mostly on white Texans without a college degree, who back him 68 percent to 29 percent. White college graduates are essentially a coin flip at 47 percent for Hinojosa and 46 percent for Abbott. Republican strategist Mike Madrid, who has spent years tracking Hispanic voting behavior, said the numbers reflect something the political establishment has been slow to grasp. "People, I think, broadly are failing to understand that the Latino vote is the largest swing vote in America," Madrid told Newsweek in an interview. Democrats are running a little better in the Senate race. Talarico leads Paxton 50 percent to 44 percent in the same poll, and he wins 97 percent of Harris voters to Hinojosa's 95 percent. Abbott, meanwhile, holds 84 percent of 2024 Trump voters, two points more than Paxton. One caveat on the comparison: YouGov allocated undecided voters in the Senate question but did not do so for governor, which helps explain why 5 percent remain undecided there compared with 3 percent in the Senate race. Then there is Trump. Only 44 percent of Texas likely voters approve of the job he is doing, and 51 percent strongly disapprove, in a sample that says it backed him over Kamala Harris by 12 points in 2024. What Earlier Polls Show Which candidate is ahead depends a lot on which pollster you read. In June, a New York Times/Siena College poll of 656 likely voters found Abbott with the backing of 51 percent of voters and Hinojosa with 44 percent. When Times/Siena went back into the field from September 21 to 30, Hinojosa led 49 percent to 46 percent among 615 likely voters. Marist University's September 17 to 20 survey of 1,139 registered voters landed on the same 49-46 result. ReconMR and the Siena Research Institute also showed Hinojosa leading 49 percent to 45 percent, a reversal from July, when the same poll had Abbott ahead by a single point. The Fox News poll, conducted by Beacon Research and Shaw & Company Research from September 24 to 28, put Abbott up 52 percent to 47 percent among 881 likely voters. Big Data Poll and Slingshot Strategies each had the governor ahead by 4 or 5 points, as did a Stratus Intelligence poll paid for by the Republican group Texans for a Conservative Majority. In between sit an N+ Univision/YouGov poll that found the two candidates deadlocked at 47 percent and an Overton Insights/Texas Public Policy Foundation survey with Abbott ahead 46.9 percent to 45.8 percent. Over the summer, the governor's cushion was wider. Abbott led by 7 points in a University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll in early June, and a late July Texas Southern University poll found him leading 49 percent to 43 percent. No public poll since mid-September has shown him up by more than 5. A Blue Texas? It Might Happen Democrats have been promising a breakthrough in Texas for three decades. No Democrat has won statewide office there since 1994, and Trump carried the state by 13 points in 2024. Abbott beat Beto O'Rourke by roughly 11 points in 2022. Hinojosa is a different kind of candidate from O'Rourke. A civil rights and union lawyer who grew up in the Rio Grande Valley, she made her name in the Texas House as the chief antagonist of Abbott's school voucher push, and her campaign has since widened its focus to grocery bills, data centers and what she calls corruption in the governor's office. "Every poll tells the same story: Texans are tired of working more and getting less," Hinojosa said over the summer. Her numbers among Hispanic voters, who swung toward Republicans in 2024, may matter most. Madrid said Washington misread what happened in 2024. "Most people were thinking it was part of this permanent realignment. A lot of people who understand the Latino vote were saying it's not that at all," he said. Independents are also drifting her way, according to ReconMR, which found her with large leads in Austin, Dallas-Fort Worth and San Antonio and Abbott ahead in rural areas. Abbott keeps the upper hand on the issues Republicans have run on for a decade. On securing the border, voters picked him over Hinojosa 53 percent to 39 percent, and he led on keeping Texans safe, while she led on making prices more affordable. He also has far more money. At the end of June, Abbott had about $67 million on hand to Hinojosa's $3 million, though she has said her campaign raised $20 million since January. The Latest on the Race There may never be a debate. Hinojosa accepted an invitation for a one-hour debate on Thursday, October 15, in Fort Worth, hosted by NBCUniversal Television Stations Texas and Hearst Newspapers Texas and broadcast in English and Spanish. Her campaign says Abbott let the deadline pass, and that he also ignored a September debate hosted by Nexstar. Abbott's team has preferred social media. The governor recently posted an image of Hinojosa as a Lotería card, the Mexican bingo game. Campaign spokesperson Eduardo Leal defended the post, calling Hinojosa an "out-of-touch Democrat socialist." From the Hinojosa side, the reply was an invitation. Abbott "has to lie because he's been governor for 12 years," spokesperson Tommy Kubischek said, adding that the governor should make his case at a debate. Hinojosa is also courting voters well outside her party. At the Texas Tribune Festival, she unveiled an ad featuring Lynn Davenport, a self-described MAGA conservative who believed the 2020 election was stolen and now says she will vote for the Democrat. Abbott was invited to the festival and didn't respond. What Happens Next Early voting begins October 19 and ends October 30. Election Day is November 3, and the Fort Worth debate, whether Abbott shows up or not, comes four days before the first ballots are cast. Turnout could decide it. The groups carrying Hinojosa in the YouGov poll, younger voters and Hispanic voters, tend to skip midterms at higher rates than the older white Texans who make up Abbott's base. And the governor has the money to stay on television through the final stretch. Hinojosa's fate may be tied to Talarico's. A Senate race that drives Democratic-leaning voters to the polls would help her more than anything her own campaign can buy.
news.summary: A new YouGov poll has Democratic state Representative Gina Hinojosa narrowly ahead of Greg Abbott.
news.author: Jesus Mesa

news.title: 'Top Gun: Maverick' Star Glen Powell Explains Why He Doesn't Preach Politics: It Divides People
news.text:
The Twisters star Glen Powell says he is not interested in speaking out about politics because the discussion alienates too many people.

In an interview with Esquire magazine, Powell says that his parents were utterly disinterested in politics. And these days, the Chad Powers star says that politics interests him even less, the magazine says.

To Powell, politics are just too divisive.

“Over time, I realized that politics divide people,” he told the magazine.

“People trying to prove their point — for me, it’s the worst version of a conversation,” he continued. “I genuinely do not like the discourse.”

“It’s not as healthy as it once was,” he said, adding that talking politics “is not presently possible. I applaud people for jumping into those things and fighting for what they believe in. If I were a political person, I would be talking about it. For me, my calling is elsewhere.”

Powell has had a series of high-profile roles over the last decade, in films including Top Gun: Maverick, Twisters, and The Running Man. And he has scored a big streaming hit with his football comedy series, Chad Powers, a series he also created along with Michael Waldron.

Powell joins what might be a growing list of actors and entertainers who have finally learned the lesson that speaking out about politics naturally ticks off half their potential fan base.

Action star Dwayne Johnson, for one, learned that lesson after suffering a huge backlash for endorsing Joe Biden, even as he had previously claimed to lean to the center in political ideology. After that debacle, by July of this year, Johnson was pledging to steer clear of politics on the future.

“I’ve learned I’m going to keep my politics to myself. There are moments when, hey, there’s nothing we can’t talk about. If I’m wrong, I’ll tell you I’m wrong. Or if I feel like I got a leg up and this is the right way to go, I’ll share it with you. Politics is omnipresent and it’s forever. I don’t like it. I hate it at times. I hate the slinging. I hate all the bullshit that comes with it,” he said.

After being blasted for supporting Biden, “The Rock” quickly pivoted and refused to make any endorsements when the Democrat Party abandoned Biden and switched allegiance to Kamala Harris.

“My goal is to bring this country together. I believe in that. There will be no endorsement. At this level of influence, I will keep my politics to myself. It is between me and the ballot box,” he said when the party coronated Harris for the 2024 presidential election.

Another top celebrity who recently began backing away from politics is Jennifer Lawrence.

Despite previous vitriolic attacks on Republicans and Donald Trump, the Hunger Games star did an about face late last year by stating that expounding on politics was just making things worse.

Last November, Lawrence said that she has come to the opinion that spouting off about politics does not make a difference. “So, then what am I doing? I’m just sharing my opinion on something that’s going to add fuel to a fire that’s ripping the country apart. We are so divided,” she said.

Others who are begging off on politics include Josh Duhamel, who said actors should avoid upsetting half their audience by talking about politics, and Kevin James, who said he leaves politics to people who are more informed on the issues than he.

news.title: Swing Voters Have Buyer’s Remorse Over Trump — And 1 Candidate Could Get Hit Hard
news.text:
Some Michigan residents who voted for President Donald Trump in the last presidential election expressed buyer’s remorse on Tuesday during an MS NOW focus group.

Multiple swing voters who spoke to the network said they are not willing to vote for Trump-backed Senate candidate Mike Rogers next month over Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed.

“I was surprised that there wasn’t more support or more leaning Rogers in that group,” MS NOW analyst Elise Jordan said after the interviews aired. “You know, these cross-pressure voters, but then you look at some of the polling, and Abdul El-Sayed is pulling more from Trump voters at around 8% than, likewise, than Rogers pulling about 5% of Kamala Harris voters.”

During one panel, she asked the group, “What were you hoping [Trump] would change?”

“I thought, like, run it like a business, more like not just like your family, like bring more in for us for the Americans, get our economy up, and like run it like he wants America to be a wealthy business,” one voter said. “But I just think now it’s a Trump, it’s a Trump business.”

Another Trump voter said she had strong hopes he would make changes in foreign affairs, but she is now “very disappointed.”

“He’s a good liar,” another voter in the room chimed in. 

Rogers, along with other Republican candidates in the midterms, is facing challenges because of his alignment with Trump, whose favorability is sinking as Americans grow sour over the war in Iran and the administration’s handling of the economy. 

A recent Fox News poll shows El-Sayed leading the race with 50%, a slim point above Rogers’ 49%, among likely voters. 

When asked if they would vote for Rogers in the upcoming election, few raised their hands. 

One person who raised her hand for El-Sayed declared, “If I don’t vote for him, I’m not voting.”

“That’s how I would be too. I wouldn’t vote for Mike Rogers,” another voter said.

A voter who raised her hand for Rogers clarified that she’s “not happy about it, but there again, it’s either vote or don’t vote.”

news.title: 'The panic is palpable': El-Sayed facing opposition from key Michigan Democrat groups weeks before election
news.text:
While polling suggests Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is leading the Senate race in Michigan, members of key Democrat-leaning demographics say he hasn't earned their votes, even as absentee ballots have already begun to trickle in.

Like others in the Rust Belt, Michigan is a purple state. Michigan voted for President Donald Trump in 2016 and 2024, but went for President Joe Biden in 2020. It also currently has a Democrat executive branch and state Senate but a Republican House.

'The exodus of Jewish and black Democrats from Conman Abdul El-Sayed's camp exposes his crumbling coalition.'

While Trump won Michigan in 2024, Vice President Kamala Harris carried Wayne County, which includes Detroit, and Oakland County, which has a high Jewish population. That same year, Democrat Elissa Slotkin barely squeaked by Republican Mike Rogers in the U.S. Senate race by just 0.34%.

So it's no wonder that in 2026, El-Sayed and Rogers are in a tough battle for the open seat soon to be vacated by Democrat Sen. Gary Peters.

As of Wednesday afternoon, Blaze News Poll Watch has El-Sayed with an edge of 2.6%, and, according to CNN, El-Sayed has already predicted he will win by seven points.

Yet frank admissions by high-profile Michigan Democrats as well as black and Jewish voters suggest he may actually have some ground to make up in his own party.

RELATED: ‘Not someone who can be trusted’: Anti-Trump Detroit newspaper rips El-Sayed in Rogers endorsement

Democrat Rep. Hillary Scholten, who represents a district in Western Michigan, was caught on a video dated September 26 admitting that the El-Sayed campaign still has a lot of work to do "to connect with the black community."

In an MS NOW clip that went viral this week, one black female said, "We don't know him," while another said: "He's taking advantage that we, as black people, are Democratic, and he think we're gonna vote for him anyway, and I'm like, 'No, sir.'"

An MS NOW panel of pro-Israel Democrats similarly expressed skepticism of El-Sayed — with good reason. 

A former staffer for his campaign is under federal indictment in connection with anti-Semitic attacks, his family members have been linked to Islamic terrorist groups, and he infamously responded to the Hezbollah-inspired attack on Temple Israel in March by saying, "Hurt people hurt people."

"I can't vote for Abdul El-Sayed because, once again, he's going against something that's innately me," said one Jewish mother.

"I might go to Mike Rogers," said another.

Lansing Mayor Andy Schor, who is Jewish, indicated that the El-Sayed team has not made overtures for his support and that he may ultimately not vote for him. "If he doesn’t need me, he doesn’t need me," Schor stated, according to CNN.

Democrat Attorney General Dana Nessel, who is also Jewish, initially distanced herself from El-Sayed but ultimately endorsed him.

In the last week, Blaze News has received multiple text messages from Nonnegotiable Michigan, a group of Democrat-voting Jews in Michigan who launched a month ago in part to "call on El-Sayed and Democratic candidates to affirm baseline commitments to Jewish safety and identity."

"We've always shown up overwhelmingly for Democrats — but our support requires us to feel safe and valued in the party that has been our political home," read a message delivered Sunday.

Scholten and the El-Sayed campaign did not respond to requests for comment from Blaze News.

RELATED: Obama rushes to rescue Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit — GOP issues scathing response

Greg Manz, senior communications director for the Michigan GOP, characterized El-Sayed as a "conman" who "has repeatedly brushed off concerns from black voters" even as he is being "bankrolled by elements tied to the Muslim Brotherhood."

"The exodus of Jewish and black Democrats from Conman Abdul El-Sayed's camp exposes his crumbling coalition," Manz said in a statement to Blaze News.

"The panic is palpable."

news.title: Media Research Center: Apple News Hid Stories Reporting on DNC's Financial Woes Ahead of Midterms
news.text:
Apple News hid stories that reported on the weak financial condition of the Democratic National Committee (DNC) is ahead of the midterm elections, according to the Media Research Center.

Media Research Center (MRC) identified 78 stories about the DNC’s mounting debt, finding that none of them were promoted on Apple News’ top 20 stories from January 1 through September 28, according to the analysis, obtained by the New York Post.

Notably, September 28 marks just five weeks before the 2026 midterm elections — and nearly a year after the DNC disclosed that it is in millions of dollars in debt.

“Apple isn’t curating the news,” MRC President David Bozell said. “It’s running a high-tech protection racket for the political left.”

The MRC found that at least 14 stories about the DNC’s debt from outlets that Apple News typically promotes were also not featured, including USA Today, the Guardian, the New York Times, the Washington Post, the Wall Street Journal, and Politico.

“Our study found Apple News suppressing coverage of the Democratic Party’s fundraising woes while eagerly serving up stories damaging to Republicans,” Bozell told the Post, adding that stories promoted by the service can generate anywhere from 1 million to 20 million page views.

Interestingly, Apple News uses human editors to select many of the stories that appear on its platform — unlike Google News and Microsoft’s MSN, which depend heavily on algorithms to select and arrange stories.

Late last year, the DNC blamed its nearly $16 million debt on the ill-fated 2024 Biden-Harris campaign. From there, Kamala Harris’ failed 2024 presidential reportedly campaign spent around $1.5 billion.

By the end of it, the Democratic National Committee was left with $20.5 million in debt. then, in October 2025, the DNC took out a $15 million loan for gubernatorial elections.

The DNC rang in 2026 with $17.5 million in debt, according to a report by the New York Times. Meanwhile, the Republican National Committee (RNC) has $230 million in the bank and no debt.

“For years, the media lectured Americans about ‘dirty money in politics’ whenever Republicans had the fundraising advantage,” Bozell told the Post. “Now Democrats are facing a financial mess of their own making, and suddenly the story isn’t worth telling.”

As Breitbart News reported, the DNC’s financial woes have sparked calls to oust DNC Chairman Ken Martin, who has found himself increasingly isolated, throwing a phone at a junior aide’s desk in frustration.

Alana Mastrangelo-Wrask is a reporter for Breitbart News. You can follow her on Facebook and X at @ARmastrangelo, and on Instagram.

news.title: Democrats' Blue Wave Could Miss New York
news.text: Democrats enter the final weeks of the 2026 midterms with favorable tailwinds as voters sour on President Donald Trump, but polls suggest the party may not be matching its national momentum in New York, the state that experienced the nation’s largest rightward shift in 2024. With less than four weeks until the November 3 midterm elections, Democrats are expanding their lead nationally and are working to expand the electoral battleground to compete in more conservative states like Alaska, Iowa, Kansas and Texas. But two recent surveys have produced underwhelming results for Democrats in New York, long seen as a major progressive stronghold, raising questions about whether the "blue wave” will manifest itself in the Empire State. As Democrats expand their lead on the national generic ballot, that has not translated into gains in New York, with recent polls showing Democrats up between 11 and 13 points in the state. The polls could signal a worrying trend for New York Democrats. Former Vice President Kamala Harris won the state by fewer than 13 points in 2024, down from former President Joe Biden’s 23-point victory in 2020. No other state saw a larger jump to the right in the most recent presidential race. The trend was driven by Trump’s inroads among Hispanic and Asian American voters, as well as more stagnant suburbs outside of New York City. That rightward shift also showed up further down the ballot, with Democrats winning the generic congressional vote by 15 points, down from 24 points in 2020, according to SplitTicket. Boris Heersink, a political science professor at Fordham University, told Newsweek that if Trump’s 2024 coalition lasted in New York, it could “produce an environment where a particularly appealing Republican could do well” in the state. But he also said that does not “seem to be the most likely outcome.” “I don't think the current polls suggest a long-term trend away from the Democrats. What I think is clear is that the era where Democrats were completely dominating New York in the 2010s is over,” he said. New York Polls Show Democrats Lagging National Gains Recent polling data suggest Democrats are struggling to rebuild their dominance in New York politics, even in a more favorable environment ahead of the midterm elections, though it could ultimately come down to how undecided voters break between now and November 3. These polls still give Democrats a statewide advantage. Democrats led Republicans on the generic ballot by only 13 points, 55 percent to 42 percent, in a new Marist University poll of New York registered voters. Meanwhile, in the gubernatorial race, Democratic Governor Kathy Hochul led her Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman, the Nassau County executive, by only 11 points, 53 percent to 42 percent. The poll surveyed 1,361 registered voters from October 1 to 4 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.6 percentage points. Just weeks earlier, a Siena University poll produced similarly concerning results for Democrats. It found Democrats leading the generic ballot by only 11 points, 51 percent to 40 percent, while Hochul was up only 9 points, 50 percent to 41 percent. The poll surveyed 1,144 likely voters from September 11 to 17, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.2 percentage points. However, a recent Quinnipiac University poll was a bit better for Hochul, showing her up 19 points, 58 percent to 39 percent. It polled 1,026 likely voters from September 17 to 20 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.1 percentage points. Historically, New York has shifted against Republican presidents. In 2018, Democrats won the generic ballot by 31 points in New York, a shift from a 22-point win in 2016. How New York Compares With National Polling At the same time, Democrats are in a strong position on the generic ballot. RealClearPolitics gives Democrats a 7.8-point lead in their aggregate, while Nate Silver showed Democrats up 9 points as of Wednesday. That marks a notable shift from 2024, when Republicans won the generic ballot by 2.7 points. Polling shifts have been driven by a decline in Trump’s approval rating. Historically, when the president is unpopular ahead of the midterms, his party tends to lose seats in the House and Senate. Democrats have sought to make the midterms a referendum on Trump as he faces voter backlash over the economy, cost of living and high gas prices amid the Iran war. But midterm shifts are not always even, and some polling suggests other Democratic states like Massachusetts and Oregon are also not seeing significant leftward trends this year. Meanwhile, races in states like Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas, which backed Trump by double digits in 2024, appear more competitive. New York voters have a “long-standing and deep frustration” with state-level politics, which may help explain why polls show the state is closer than expected in the midterms, Grant Davis Reeher, a political science professor at Syracuse University, told Newsweek. “Affordability here is just as likely to focus on the state’s high taxes and spending as on the price of gas and eggs,” he said. “That provides avenues for Republicans to make a case, at least, even in a very blue state. In addition, most of the Republicans that are left in office, or that are running, are more moderate than the typical Republican, and especially the MAGA Republican.” What This Means for Key Midterm Races Hochul remains the favorite to win reelection, as she has not trailed a single public poll. The Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball both consider the race to be solid or safe for Democrats. New York has some important congressional races. In New York’s 3rd District, Democratic Representative Tom Suozzi is facing a challenge from Republican State Assemblymember Mike LePetri. Democrats are also hoping to flip New York’s 17th District, a Harris-won seat held by GOP Representative Mike Lawler. Democrats are running Cait Conley in that race. These are two seats that could determine whether Democrats or Republicans will control the House of Representatives after the midterms. Reeher said he doubts that Democrats will lose any seats at the federal level in New York. “At the state and local level, you might see some upsets, if local issues can combine with a lesser blue wave at the top of the ticket to produce the right formula,” Reeher said. Ciro Riccardi, a spokesperson for Lawler’s campaign, pointed to Hochul as a vulnerability for New York Democrats. "She is deeply underwater with independents and in the suburbs thanks to her policies: sanctuary laws that protect criminals, sky-high taxes, and non-stop utility bill increases approved by her PSC,” Riccardi said. Conley’s “refusal to campaign publicly with Hochul tells you everything you need to know about Hochul’s impact on down ballot races,” he said. In a statement to Newsweek, the LePetri campaign said that “all politics are local” and that Democrats in New York “no longer work for the people.” “Taxin’ Tom Suozzi voted against the largest working families tax cut in history and voted to allow men in girls sports. Meanwhile Horrible Hochul is driving up utility costs and driving out businesses and young people. The last piece of the ‘Terrible Trifecta’ is Zohran ‘Commie’ Mamdani whose disastrous socialist policies are right here in NY-03 in northeast Queens and the DSA is pledging to bring more of it to Nassau County,” the statement reads. A Hochul campaign spokesperson told Newsweek that the governor is “continuing to build momentum as we near Election Day." “Bruce Blakeman has spent his failing campaign tying himself to an unpopular Trump, saying high gas prices aren’t a ‘New York issue,’ the governor’s moratorium on data centers is ‘crazy,’ and that ICE has done a ‘very, very good job,’” the spokesperson said. Newsweek also reached out to the Blakeman, Conley and Suozzi campaigns for comment. Progressives Surge in New York City—Is That Alienating Moderates? Despite Republicans making some inroads in the Empire State, New York City has become a progressive stronghold over the past few years, defined by Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s victory in the 2025 race against former Governor Andrew Cuomo and Republican Curtis Sliwa. In 2026, progressives, including Democratic socialists, gained ground in New York. Candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila-Chevalier, along with progressive Brad Lander, won Democratic primaries in House races. Avila-Chevalier and Lander unseated more moderate incumbents, major victories for the left. The DSA also won major victories in local races, as well, and have become a power player in New York politics. Some Democrats, however, have raised concerns that DSA’s rise could alienate more moderate Democrats and independents, even in cases where Democratic candidates are more moderate, such as Hochul, Suozzi or Conley. Suozzi warned that there is “little support” for their ideas in remarks to Fox News Digital in August. “Much like the Republicans have had to deal with the Freedom Caucus, the Democrats are going to have to deal with this group,” Suozzi told the outlet. Heersink said it is “very difficult” to know if the progressive surge is actually harming other Democrats. “Moderate Democrats always have a tendency to blame any underperformance on people in their party pushing them to the left. There may very well be some voters who are traditionally Democrats who do not like Mamdani and what he represents,” he said. “But there's also the potential counter-side that the DSA wing of the party is able to bring out younger voters.” A plurality of New Yorkers, 43 percent, view DSA unfavorably, compared to just 29 percent who view it favorably, according to the Quinnipiac poll. Those numbers are even lower outside of the city. In the suburbs, 26 percent of voters view DSA favorably, compared with 23 percent upstate, the poll found. What Happens Next How New York votes in November, as well as in the 2028 election, will be watched as a critical gauge of the state’s political future. Key metrics to watch could include the outcome in suburban regions on Long Island and in the Hudson River Valley, as well as how Hispanic and Asian American neighborhoods in New York City vote. As for New York's political future, the state is unlikely to be competitive in 2028, Reeher said. “I have a hard time imagining New York to be in serious play at the presidential level anytime soon,” he said. news.summary: New York swung to the right more than any state in 2024. Now, polls show Democrats' momentum may be trailing in the Empire State.

news.title: Trump Voters Back Abdul El-Sayed 5 to 1 in Live TV Panel Poll
news.text: A televised MSNOW panel of 10 Trump voters favored Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed over Republican Mike Rogers. El-Sayed is running against Rogers in a closely watched midterm race considered a key battleground, as the Democrats bid to take control of the Senate this November. Six participants said they had decided how they would vote in the race. Five raised their hands for El-Sayed, while one backed Rogers. The remaining four in the small sample were undecided, although one said she leaned “heavily” toward Rogers. If all four undecided voters ultimately supported Rogers, the panel would have been evenly divided, with five voters backing each candidate. Newsweek reached out to El-Sayed and Rogers’ campaigns for comment, via email and online contact form, respectively, on Wednesday. MSNOW’s Elise Jordan also asked those backing El-Sayed how firmly they had settled on their choice. “Pretty firm,” responded one. “I’m about 90 percent,” said another, adding: “If I don’t vote for him, I’m not voting.” The panelists were also asked what changes they had hoped Trump would bring about when they voted for him in 2024. “I think a lot of people looked at his 2016 win and how much better the country was before [COVID-19], and hoped that it would replicate that,” one responded. “To me it doesn’t seem like it has.” El-Sayed to Campaign with Obama in Michigan El-Sayed announced on Monday that former President Barack Obama would campaign alongside him in Detroit later this month. “It is my honor and privilege to announce that [Obama] is joining us on the trail in Detroit on Saturday, October 24,” El-Sayed wrote on X. Former Vice President Kamala Harris made a joint appearance with El-Sayed last month. Michigan Senate Race: Latest Polls Three recent Michigan polls placed El-Sayed just ahead of Rogers in a tight Senate race. A Quantus Insights survey of 762 likely voters published Wednesday placed El-Sayed at 47.6 percent and Rogers at 46.5 percent. The poll had a margin of error of approximately plus or minus 7.8 points. A YouGov poll conducted between September 22 and October 4 among 3,949 likely voters put El-Sayed at 49 percent and Rogers at 48 percent. This survey had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.5 percentage points. Meanwhile, polling conducted by Mitchell Research and Communications for CBS News Detroit placed El-Sayed at 45.6 percent and Rogers at 41.4 percent. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points and was conducted among more than 680 likely voters. Trump’s Approval in Michigan As Newsweek reported on Wednesday, recent polling data from research firm Civiqs showed President Donald Trump’s approval stood at -26 points in the key battleground state, which backed Trump by less than 2 points in 2024. El-Sayed’s Past Citizenship Remarks The Washington Free Beacon reported on Monday that video from a 2016 medical conference in Detroit showed Abdul El-Sayed saying he carried dual citizenship in the U.S. and Egypt. The outlet said the footage was the second known instance in which El-Sayed had described himself as a dual citizen, after it previously reported that a 2014 academic résumé listed him as a citizen of both countries. His campaign reportedly previously told the Free Beacon that El-Sayed had never held dual citizenship and had mistakenly believed otherwise based on information passed down by relatives. The outlet said his campaign did not respond to questions about the reported 2016 remarks. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. news.title: Trump makes late Nobel Prize pitch: ‘Not bragging ... but I settled eight wars’
news.text:
Donald Trump re-issued his call for the Nobel Prize committee to award him with the Nobel Peace Prize on Wednesday as he leaned back into talk of his peacemaking efforts.

Those peacemaking efforts, he says, are ongoing and will soon include “another one” — even though there’s no signs yet of meaningful progress in talks between the U.S. and Iran regarding another ceasefire.

The president spoke to reporters at an announcement on his “Trump accounts” for children, after returning to Washington from a spree of campaign appearances across the country.

“I’ve done stuff that nobody else has ever done. I’m not bragging, I’m just telling you the facts,” the president told reporters on Wednesday. “No president has probably ever settled any wars. I settled 8 wars."

He then went after his predecessor, Barack Obama, whom he accused of not knowing why he’d received the 2009 Peace prize. The foundation in charge of awarding the prize gave the 2009 peace prize to Obama, then less than a year into his presidency, for his diplomatic efforts to reestablish ties with the Muslim world after nearly a decade of warfare in Iraq and Afghanistan led to a perception held by some that America was at war with the entire Muslim world.

The 47th president said on Wednesday that he was more deserving of the prize than Obama.

“Look, Obama got it, and he didn’t do anything-- he still doesn’t know what he got it for,” said Trump. “He got it when he was elected, right? Right at the beginning.”

“Whether I get it or not, I have done far more [than anyone else],” the president said.

The president frequently cites the “eight wars” statistic as a reference for his supposed peacemaking abilities, but the figure is not true. Several of the “wars” on Trump’s list were not wars at all, such as disagreements between Serbia and Kosovo which never escalated to real armed conflict during either of Trump’s two presidencies. Another one of the eight is the conflict between Iran and Israel, which very much remains ongoing as part of a three-way conflict also now involving the U.S. — that conflict has been ongoing for nearly eight months.

The Iran conflict has largely shattered Trump’s image as a steward of global affairs in the minds of his own supporters, who embraced that depiction of the president during his 2024 campaign for a second term as he hammered Joe Biden and Kamala Harris over Israel’s war against Gaza and the ongoing conflict in Ukraine, both of which he pledged to end.

A year and a half after coming to power, Trump has made little to no progress in his efforts to negotiate an end to the war between Russia and Ukraine. A ceasefire exists in the Gaza Strip, where the majority of fighting has died down, but most Gazans remain in appalling conditions with much of the region’s infrastructure and housing destroyed. Israeli strikes continue to be carried out on camps of refugees, with continued civilian casualties.

The president’s touting of his diplomatic credentials also ignore one truth about his 2024 campaign: his promise to stop getting the U.S. into endless wars with murky objectives. His critics, both within and outside of the Republican Party, now accuse him of doing just that as the war in Iran has shifted from an effort to dislodge the Iranian government and take control of its remaining nuclear materials to ending disruptions over shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

Obama has long been a fixation of Trump’s, however, and the president attacks him nearly as frequently as he attacks Biden, who defeated him in the 2020 election. On Wednesday, he warned that his allies wanted to see the Justice Department wielded against Obama, Biden and Hillary Clinton, but claimed that he was respecting the sanctity of his office by declining.

We have to get rid of-- no nuclear weapons for, as you know, for Iran,” said the president. “We've taken away their nuclear power. news.title: El-Sayed Is Aiming To Unify Michigan. There's One Unknown That Could Cost Him.
news.text:
WARREN, Mich. — Democrats are a little less worried about Abdul El-Sayed these days, even if they still can’t stop arguing about him.

The progressive Senate candidate, who won an $81 million battle against moderate Rep. Haley Stevens to claim the party’s nomination for U.S. Senate in August, spent months fighting concerns about his electability and whether he could unite a splintered Democratic Party. 

But as he campaigned with the more moderate Sen. Elissa Slotkin and held town halls in a majority-Black city and a quintessential swing county over the weekend, the uber-confident El-Sayed’s certainty of victory seemed to have spread to the rest of his party. Still, loud holdouts remain, and concerns persist about GOP candidate Mike Rogers’ spending advantages in the state, with a media-buying source saying Republicans are expected to outspend Democrats by more than $20 million in the final weeks of the contest.

Asked if he was concerned about party unity, El-Sayed responded: “Of course.” But in an interview, he made clear his goal was broader.

“My goal is to unite the state around this campaign,” he told HuffPost. “We all understand, even if we had our differences in the primary, that what we’re up against is a lot worse than anything that divided us.”

And while El-Sayed’s progressive policies — including his support for “Medicare for All” and opposition to aid to Israel — defined much of his primary campaign, his efforts against Rogers have largely been in step with other Democratic campaigns, relentlessly focused on corruption, affordability and the link between the two.

Polling indicates the efforts are working, with El-Sayed consistently holding a slight lead over Rogers. He’s also continuing to get backup from national party figures: After former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned for him in September, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani appeared at a fundraiser for him on Monday, just hours after President Barack Obama announced a campaign event for later this month.

And while Rogers’ campaign has made a significant show of reaching out to Democrats, polling gives little indication there are many defectors: a New York Times survey found just 3% of Democrats and 5% of those who backed Harris in 2024 were voting for the Republican, while El-Sayed was picking up 8% of those who supported Trump two years ago and dominating among those who didn’t cast a ballot.

This has led some of El-Sayed’s earlier detractors to admit his relative strengths: The Never-Trump Republican pollster Sarah Longwell marveled at his ability to win over Trump voters in a recent piece, and Center for American Progress President Neera Tanden — arguably Stevens’ biggest online booster — praised El-Sayed’s ability to unite the party during a Monday night appearance on CNN. 

At the same time, the symbolism of a potential El-Sayed win, highlighted by Ocasio-Cortez’s prediction at Monday’s fundraiser that his victory would “break open the entire political calculus in America,” essentially guarantees his candidacy will remain a political football in the never-ending back-and-forth between the party’s progressive and moderate wings. 

Rogers’ campaign did not respond to repeated requests for comment.

The enthusiasm for El-Sayed among some Michiganders was apparent standing in the back of a Flint, Michigan, church on Saturday, where supporters carrying signs and wearing football jerseys emblazoned with his name crammed into the sanctuary. The candidate, wearing a black, long-sleeve shirt under a suit jacket that he quickly shed as he took the stage, stayed issues-focused as he answered questions about Social Security, the cost of living and corruption in the Trump administration.

“A lot of the pundits — you know — the people on TV who are smarter than the rest of us, they’re always like, ‘he can’t win,’” El-Sayed told one supporter. “It’s like they think that people out here are running around thinking, ‘Where do I fit on the left-right spectrum? Is he a little bit too far to the left for me?’ I think most people are running around thinking, ‘How am I going to afford my rent, my car, my insurance and my groceries?’”

Speaking to HuffPost in an interview following the event, El-Sayed reiterated that he thought the popular momentum was behind him. “We know that the Trump agenda is devastating Michiganders,” he said. “I hear that from everywhere, and everybody that I talk to. You see the excitement here on the ground.”

Later that day, El-Sayed made another stop at the carpenters’ union banquet hall in Warren, Detroit’s largest suburb and part of Macomb County, which decidedly backed President Donald Trump in the 2024 election. It was an event characterized by firsts — El-Sayed’s campaign had never before traveled to Warren, and he had never directly campaigned alongside Slotkin.

“We don’t agree on everything, and that’s OK,” said Slotkin. “We agree on the things that are really important: putting a check on this man in the White House who is trying to tell us America is over.”

And the sitting Michigan senator poured cold water on discussions about political rifts within her party. “The debate of moderate versus progressive is not the real debate,” she told the crowd. “The real debate among Democrats right now is fight versus flight. I need someone who is with me on ‘team fight.’”

The crowd in Warren, which filled the banquet hall to capacity, showed no signs of backing down from El-Sayed. Many voters felt his message spoke directly to them.

“We’re sick of the bullshit,” said Eric Ciaglo, a 75-year-old from Harrison, Michigan, who attended the event with his wife. “The corruption. It’s right in our face. All these years, I’ve never seen such corruption and bullshit ... and people accepting it.”

And state Rep. Mai Xiong, a Democrat who represents parts of Warren, said she thought El-Sayed was within striking distance in Macomb County, which had gone for Trump in the past three presidential elections. 

“They come here because they know that the pathway to winning runs through this community,” Xiong said, adding that she “100%” thought El-Sayed could flip the county. “To know that the Abdul campaign is hearing that and understanding the importance of picking up these votes here — that’s how we’re gonna win.” 

But behind the rosy atmosphere of El-Sayed’s campaign events, where most attendees appear to have made up their minds about casting their votes in November, there lies an undercurrent of tension, particularly among Black voters in the Detroit area who, according to state political leaders, are still wary of the Democrat after largely backing Stevens in the primary.

“I think there needs to be more solidarity with Black people,” said Kimberly Fisher, a small business owner running to represent parts of Detroit and Warren in the Michigan legislature. “Detroit is the Blackest city in the country, and there’s been no engagement.”

Anyone with worries about support for El-Sayed in Michigan’s Black communities would not have been placated by the crowds at his campaign events in Warren and Flint. Though the latter city’s population is 56% Black, the crowd gathered at St. Michael’s Conference Center was mostly white.

Fisher, who has a longstanding relationship with El-Sayed and supports his campaign, told HuffPost in an interview she thought the candidate had a “passion” for the Black community in Detroit — pointing to his work expanding a municipal financial aid program for childcare and his support following a recent tornado in the area — but that she hadn’t seen that same passion on the campaign trail.

And it might be too late for him to salvage those votes, warned Fisher, who previously raised her concerns directly with El-Sayed during a town hall meeting last month. At the time, El Sayed said he wanted to “bring communities together” as the son of an immigrant who understood “the debt of gratitude I owe to Black communities who advocated for the right of my dad to even immigrate here in the first place.” 

“We’re talking months and months of missed opportunities,” Fisher said. “We’re talking about ignoring a community that is a large part of your voter base.”

Fisher said lingering tensions between Black and Arab communities are still hurting El-Sayed, with many Black people in Detroit feeling the Arab American community “looks down” on them. 

Many of the state’s Jewish voters, too, continue to find El-Sayed’s opposition to aid to Israel and belief that the country is committing a genocide in Gaza to be unacceptable. 

But while Rogers has focused extensively on El-Sayed’s foreign policy positions, there’s little indication it’s hurting the Democrat: Voters in the Times survey are split on who they trust more to handle the Israel-Palestine conflict, but say they would prefer a candidate who opposes aid to Israel by a 38% to 29% margin over one who supports it.

news.title: Michigan's Mike Rogers Seizes on October 7 Anniversary to Attack El-Sayed
news.text: Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers used the third anniversary of the October 7 Hamas attacks in Israel to attack Democratic rival Abdul El-Sayed, accusing him of spreading antisemitism and sympathizing with terrorists. In a statement Wednesday, Rogers accused El-Sayed of fundraising off October 7, campaigning with progressive commentator Hasan Piker and appearing to sympathize with the attacker who targeted Temple Israel in Michigan earlier this year. "At a time when we especially need to turn the temperature down and stand alongside our Jewish friends and neighbors, he only spreads antisemitism and incites more violence," Rogers said. The attack is part of Rogers' broader effort to make El-Sayed's views on Israel, Hamas and antisemitism a central issue in the closely watched Michigan Senate race, where Rogers has trailed in polling in the weeks leading up to the November 3 election. El-Sayed and his campaign have not yet commented on the anniversary as of Wednesday morning. Newsweek reached out to El-Sayed's campaign for comment Wednesday. Antisemitism Has Shadowed the Race Since the Primary El-Sayed, who would become the first Muslim U.S. senator if elected, has been an outspoken critic of Israel's war in Gaza, which he has described as a genocide, and has called for ending U.S. military aid to Israel. Rogers' Wednesday attack also revived a controversy from last year's anniversary. On October 7, 2025, El-Sayed's campaign, which was still in the primary race at the time, sent supporters a fundraising email criticizing Israel's ground invasion of Gaza while making no mention of the Hamas attack that preceded it. A campaign spokesperson said the email "mistakenly went out" the day before. Michigan state Senator Mallory McMorrow, then one of El-Sayed's primary rivals, called it "beyond tone deaf." Scrutiny grew over the spring, when El-Sayed rallied at the University of Michigan and Michigan State University with left-wing streamer Hasan Piker, who had called Orthodox Jews "inbred" and described Zionism as a "mental illness." Michigan Representative Haley Stevens, a Democrat and El-Sayed's rival for the Democratic nomination at the time, accused him of "choosing to campaign with someone who has a history of antisemitic rhetoric." El-Sayed later put distance between himself and Piker. Israel also dominated the money in the Democratic primary. The United Democracy Project, AIPAC's largest super PAC, spent a record $30.6 million in this race backing Stevens. El-Sayed made AIPAC and the tens of millions of dollars spent to support Stevens a centerpiece of his campaign, casting the contest as "the many versus the money." Stevens, in turn, said El-Sayed wants to "blame all of your problems on Jewish Americans." On the morning of October 7, 2023, Hamas militants fired several thousand rockets into Israel and thousands of militants attacked through holes blown in the border fence or with boats or motorized paragliders. Some 1,200 people were killed and 251 others taken hostage. Israel responded with a military offensive that has killed over 74,000 Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, according to local health authorities cited by the Associated Press, left the territory in ruins and sparked an ongoing humanitarian catastrophe. Polls Show a Tight Race in Michigan Rogers' attack comes as recent polls show El-Sayed holding a narrow edge, with several of the latest surveys putting the race within a single point. A Quantus Insights poll conducted October 5 to 6 found El-Sayed leading Rogers 48 percent to 47 percent among 744 likely voters. A YouGov survey of 3,947 likely voters, taken September 22 to October 4, showed the same 1-point margin, 49 percent to 48 percent. A Fox News poll, conducted by Beacon Research and Shaw & Company Research from September 24 to 28, also had El-Sayed up by a point, 50 percent to 49 percent among 1,028 likely voters. Trafalgar Group, a Republican-leaning firm, found him ahead 47 percent to 45 percent among 1,085 likely voters in a survey taken September 28 to 30. Other polls have given El-Sayed more breathing room. Mitchell Research & Communications found him leading 46 percent to 41 percent among 682 likely voters in an October 1 survey, while Marist University had him up 51 percent to 44 percent among 1,235 registered voters in a poll conducted September 24 to 27. The Cook Political Report rates the race a toss-up, while Decision Desk HQ lists it as leaning Democratic. Sabato's Crystal Ball moved the race from "Toss-up" to "Leans Democratic," calling El-Sayed a "soft favorite" over Rogers. Latest Developments in the Michigan Senate Race Between Mike Rogers and Abdul El-Sayed The two candidates will meet face to face for the first time Thursday in Grand Rapids, with a second debate set for October 21, moderated by Detroit station WXYZ. Rogers previewed the matchups on X, writing that Michiganders would "learn just how much of a Conman you really are." El-Sayed has nicknamed his opponent "Mike Dodgers" for ignoring earlier debate challenges. Former President Barack Obama will rally with El-Sayed and Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor, in Detroit on October 24, the Michigan Democratic Party announced Monday. The rally falls on the first day of in-person early voting in Michigan. The stop takes Obama to Detroit, where El-Sayed struggled in the Democratic primary. Detroit is more than three-quarters Black, and Obama remains highly popular there. It had been unclear whether Obama would back El-Sayed, who has called the Affordable Care Act, one of Obama's signature achievements, an "incremental" policy. El-Sayed has worked to repair divisions left by the primary. He campaigned over the weekend with Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin, a Democrat who is Jewish. Former Vice President Kamala Harris also campaigned for him in Michigan last month. El-Sayed has also reached into conservative media. On Monday, he sat for an interview with Fox News anchor Martha MacCallum, who pressed him on accepting money from wealthy donors after he had campaigned against corporate money. The interview came after a contentious 25-minute appearance with Fox News host Jesse Watters, which many media commentators viewed as a strong performance by El-Sayed. The Democratic nominee's appearances on Fox News drew President Donald Trump's anger Tuesday. In his Truth Social post, Trump complained that Fox "spends more time covering the Jihadist and Dumocrat candidates than they do the good old fashioned Republicans." Why is the Michigan Senate Race Important in the 2026 Midterms? Michigan is one of a handful of states Democrats see as central to retaking control of the Senate in 2027, and the seat is open after Senator Gary Peters announced he would not seek reelection. Republicans are defending a 53-47 Senate majority this November, while Democrats need to flip at least four Republican-held seats without losing any of their own, making Michigan one of the cycle's most closely watched contests. El-Sayed, who ran for Michigan governor in 2018 and later led the state's health department under Governor Gretchen Whitmer, has positioned himself as part of a newer generation of Democrats willing to break with the party's establishment on economic messaging. Rogers, who represented Michigan in Congress for 14 years before joining the FBI, has leaned on his federal law enforcement background and an endorsement from Trump to make the case that he can hold the seat in Republican hands. Ad spending reflects the stakes. More money has been spent in Michigan than in any other state where Republicans have a chance to gain a Senate seat, according to ad-tracking firm AdImpact. Spending by El-Sayed, Rogers and allied groups has topped $205 million, according to a review of federal records by Bridge Michigan, a nonprofit news organization. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Mike Rogers used the third anniversary of the Hamas attack to accuse Abdul El-Sayed of antisemitism in Michigan's Senate race.

news.title: Is ‘Trumpism’ to Blame for the ‘Cornell 7’ Circus?
news.text:
No national controversy is complete until Amanda Marcotte has made a fool of herself about it, and the feminist writer has gotten a good head start on the so-called “Cornell 7” case. The sordid tale of an Ivy League orgy that devolved into accusations of sexual assault prompted Marcotte to indict “Trumpism” as somehow explaining skeptical reactions to the story.

Before getting into the details of what happened to “Jane Doe” at a Cornell University frat house two years ago — or what Marcotte had to say about it — it is best to begin by recalling Marcotte’s history of error and folly. She was a mere independent feminist blogger in January 2007 when it was announced that she (along with the execrable Melissa McEwan) would be joining the Democratic presidential campaign of former North Carolina Sen. John Edwards. That gig was short-lived, as Marcotte’s previous commentary proved too controversial for Edwards, who said he was “personally offended.” (The Edwards campaign itself later collapsed in ignominy.)

Among the topics that Marcotte addressed in her (now deleted) blog was the infamous 2006 rape hoax involving Duke University lacrosse team (see my column, “The Long Shadow of a Lie: The Duke Lacrosse Rape Hoax, 20 Years Later“). After the charges against the falsely accused players were dismissed, Marcotte mockingly wrote: “Can’t a few white boys sexually assault a black woman anymore without people getting all wound up about it? So unfair.” The accuser (Crystal Mangum) was lying, and the district attorney (Mike Nifong) was corrupt, but Marcotte continued to insist that the “white boys” were guilty. Those who had defended the Duke players were “rape-loving scum,” Marcotte subsequently declared.

Marcotte has never admitted error, never apologized, and apparently never learned any lessons from that disgrace, as she later went all-in on another notorious rape hoax, the 2014 University of Virginia case that resulted in a multimillion-dollar defamation verdict against Rolling Stone magazine. In that case, an emotionally disturbed freshman student named Jackie invented a gang rape during a party at a fraternity house orchestrated by a junior named Haven Monahan. It turned out that no such party occurred on the night in question, and there was no UVA student named Haven Monahan. Jackie had created “Haven Monahan” using a fake email account and the photo of a former high school classmate who never attended UVA, in an apparent scheme to inspire jealousy in a guy she liked, but who hadn’t reciprocated her romantic interest (see “‘Hitler Made a Difference’: The Liberal Gang Rape of Journalism,” April 6, 2015).

As the Rolling Stone story unraveled in December 2014, Marcotte popped up to downplay the “media kerfuffle” over what she called “some discrepancies” in the story. Marcotte insisted that these discrepancies were “very likely to be the result of Jackie misremembering key details of the night” and lamented that “many anti-feminists have seized on these discrepancies to argue that Jackie is lying.” Marcotte was wrong and the “anti-feminists” were right, because Jackie was lying. Marcotte remained undaunted four months later, after it was proven that Jackie made up the whole rape story. Without admitting any error on her part, Marcotte proclaimed that the exposure of the UVA hoax was not a victory for “rape deniers,” as she labeled those who had doubted the Rolling Stone story from the beginning. Marcotte lamented that “anti-feminists are surely going to use this story to cast doubts on rape accusations that have nothing to do with this situation.”

Let’s be clear here: It’s the media bias, stupid.

Those whom Marcotte derides as “rape deniers” do not actually deny that rape occurs, nor are “anti-feminists” (a synonym for Republicans, in Marcotte’s lexicon) against the apprehension and punishment of rapists. What conservatives oppose, however, is the media’s habit of seizing on dubious atrocity tales to gin up a witch-hunt climate of hatred against male college students, what KC Johnson and Stuart Taylor Jr. have called the Campus Rape Frenzy. As with so many other issues, the media bias regarding sexual assault on college and university campuses is basically partisan: “Girls are getting raped by frat boys, and the only way to stop it is, VOTE DEMOCRAT!”

Such is the obvious motive for national news organizations turning the “Cornell 7” case into a cause célèbre, despite the fact that (a) it’s actually just about a handful of students and former students at an Ivy League school, and (b) the incident happened two years ago and was already the subject of extensive investigations by police, the local district attorney, and Cornell University itself. There are more than 340 million people in the United States, of whom at least 339.99 million have nothing to do with the “Cornell 7” saga, yet ABC News is running Good Morning America segments about it? 

OK, as briefly as possible: “Jane Doe” (whose identity is not actually secret) was a sophomore member of the Cornell chapter of Delta Delta Delta (“Tri-Delt”) sorority. She had a crush on Matthew Ingalls, a member of the Chi Phi fraternity. They had been texting each other and, on the evening of October 19, 2024, Ingalls invited her to a party at the Chi Phi house. “Jane” spent the early part of the evening getting drunk at the Tri-Delt house, then visited a couple of bars in downtown Ithaca before walking a mile to the Chi Phi house. It was after 11 p.m. when she arrived at Chi Phi, having already consumed 10 drinks by her own admission. She had another beer and danced for a few minutes with Ingalls before he suggested that he, “Jane” and another Chi Phi member should have a ménage à trois.

By her own admission, in a sworn statement to police, “Jane” agreed to this proposition because (a) she was really attracted to Ingalls and (b) she interpreted the invitation to such a threesome to mean that she might get to witness some guy-on-guy action between Ingalls and the other male participant, Jonathan Newell (because “Jane” is pro-LGBTQ, or maybe just kinky like that). The initial threesome ended because Ingalls was too intoxicated to continue, and fell asleep. Then “Jane” and Newell were joined by another Chi Phi brother, Gillio Lopes, for another three-way. Later, Ingalls woke up and there was yet a third three-way with Ingalls, “Jane” and Chi Phi member Winston Lee. During this roughly five-hour span, “Jane” and her male partners were using the drug ketamine.

According to the local DA, Matthew Van Houten, the sworn statement by “Jane” did not describe any actual crime: “[She] did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped. On the contrary, Jane Doe’s statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual.” No criminal charges were filed, but the university administration conducted its own investigation and issued punishments that included expelling two of the participants, suspending two other Chi Phi members, banned a fifth Chi Phi (who had already graduated) from campus, and permanently shutting down the Chi Phi fraternity chapter at Cornell.

For those readers who have been keeping count, only four Chi Phi brothers (Ingalls, Newell, Lopes and Lee) are alleged to have had sex with “Jane Doe” that night, so why is it called the “Cornell 7” case? Because three other members of the fraternity (Diego Sarabia, Scott Kretzschmar and Scott Norris) visited the room where this orgy occurred. Sarabia tried to get involved in the action, but was pushed away by “Jane Doe,” while Kretzschmar and Norris walked in, saw what was happening, decided they weren’t interested, and then walked out.

All seven of these former Chi Phi brothers were named among the defendants in a civil lawsuit filed last month on behalf of “Jane Doe.” She dropped out of Cornell after the Chi Phi orgy or, as her lawsuit describes it, “criminal sex acts” perpetrated against her, an organized “gang rape,” because she “was incapable of consenting” due to her extreme level of intoxication. It was her lawsuit that resulted in this 2024 incident belatedly becoming a national news story, and prompted New York Gov. Kathy Hochul to appoint the state Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to conduct a new investigation of the “Cornell 7” case. 

Naturally, Amanda Marcotte decided that the world needed to hear her perspective on this saga. She is 100% committed to a victimhood narrative in which conservatives are sadistic villains:

[A]ccording to some on the right, Doe has not suffered enough for reporting her alleged assault to the police and then later suing the accused, the university and the fraternity. It’s not enough that she saw no charges filed, or that reportedly only two of the accused were expelled from campus. On top of her existing pain, therefore, many of the MAGA faithful are punishing her further by calling her a liar, implying she’s a slut and even threatening to out her, which would put her personal safety at risk. Whatever their intent, by doing this, they are sending a strong message to any victim of rape who might feel tempted to seek justice: Stay silent, or you’ll be next.

Does that describe me? Or you? Or anyone else whose skepticism is aroused by various aspects of this story? Marcotte’s column includes references to Ben Shapiro and Matt Walsh, who have criticized the way the “Cornell 7” saga is being portrayed. If the media were reporting the story objectively, there would be nothing to criticize, but it is clear that most major news organization have taken the same stance as Marcotte, Hochul and James: “Jane Doe” is a victim, the seven Chi Phi brothers named as defendants in her lawsuit are all guilty of heinous crimes, and the previous investigations of the incident were basically a cover-up.

Permit me to declare my own bias: I despise everything about Cornell University and everyone associated with it. It’s the same with all our rotten “elite” universities, as I’ve been saying for years: “The Ivy League Is Decadent and Depraved.” Cornell is almost as bad as Harvard, and nearly worse than Brown. The faculty at Cornell leans so far left, they’re practically horizontal, and the students are mostly Communists, who rioted this week in support of “Jane Doe.”

Nothing makes me more uncomfortable than the idea of defending any Cornell student, much less a bunch of degenerate frat boys whose idea of a fun weekend is to load up on ketamine and run a train on any Tri-Delt who shows up for the party. Nevertheless, the frat boys aren’t worse than the rest of the students at Cornell, whose obvious motive for marching around with protest signs is because nobody ever invited them to an orgy. And whatever the controversy might be, if you ever see Amanda Marcotte on one side of an issue, you may be assured that truth and justice are on the other side. She is a reliable barometer of wrongness.

How is this about “Trumpism,” though? Cornell is a hive of leftism, and the area (Tompkins County) voted 74 percent for Kamala Harris in the 2024 election. The local DA is a Democrat, as are nearly all the administration and faculty of the university, who conducted the Title IX investigation of Chi Phi. There are no “MAGA faithful” implicated in the case. We are merely spectators at this circus.

However, everything is about Trump to those afflicted with Trump Derangement Syndrome, and Amanda Marcotte might as well be Patient Zero of that epidemic. So in her column, Marcotte brings up the E. Jean Carroll farce (as if Carroll’s claims were plausible) and then proceeds to unload this absurd paragraph:

But the past decade of Trumpism has largely been built on stirring up male anger at women’s growing equality. Paranoid and unsupported claims that women have immense power to ruin men with false accusations have been the bread-and-butter of a MAGA media industry designed to exploit men’s resentment for profit. Their audiences yearn to hear that Jane Doe is the real bad guy here, and so attacking her without a single shred of real evidence against her is an opportunity that many right-wing pundits can’t seem to pass up.

Ah, “the bread-and-butter of a MAGA media industry”! Pardon me if I’m exploiting your resentment for profit, guys, but have you considered the possibility that Amanda Marcotte is wrong? Because she’s always wrong about everything, and if she is on the side of “Jane Doe,” the smart move is to assume that, indeed, “Jane Doe is the real bad guy here.”

These are the rules, and while Marcotte goes around accusing others of anger, paranoia, and resentment, those terms much more describe her and her fellow witches in the feminist coven. For the past decade, they have been seething in rage because Trump beat Hillary Clinton in 2016, thereby depriving them of the First Female President they’d been promised (as the logical sequel to the First Black President). Feminists have been craving vengeance ever since, and ruining the lives of a few Cornell students is mere collateral damage — a few minor casualties — compared to the massive harm they’ve inflicted on other targets of their wrath.

Nothing feminists have done in their decade-long crusade against what Marcotte calls “Trumpism” has really helped women. Their agenda is entirely destructive in its intentions and results, and rallying in support of “Jane Doe” is not really about helping the former sorority girl, whose reputation is permanently ruined no matter what happens with her lawsuit. No, like everything else feminists have done for the past ten years, the “Cornell 7” fury is about trying to satisfy their appetite for vengeance. But their appetite is limitless, and as soon as they’re done with this episode, they’ll go hunting for new targets to destroy.

None of what they’re doing now will change anything. When it’s all said and done, Trump will still be president, Hillary will never be president, and Amanda Marcotte will always be wrong about everything. Bet on it.
